The entry point into `src/ComputeSharp.Core/Intrinsics/Hlsl.g.cs` is very narrow: line 6 enters the `ComputeSharp` namespace, and line 9 reaches `partial class Hlsl`. When an external search leads to `Hlsl`, stop at these two locations first. The method declarations in the file then provide the surface for name-based lookup by callers.

```text
ComputeSharp
    |
    +-- Hlsl
          |
          +-- Static method declarations
```

This relationship describes only the hierarchy visible in this file. The index is kept in the form "type location—method signature—line number", making it easy to return here from a specific symbol while reading code, rather than grouping widely separated declarations into one section by functional name.

## Initial Anchors

The first recorded declaration near the beginning of the file is:

```csharp
public static int Abs(int x) => default;
```

It is on line 21. This entry should retain the full signature: the method name is `Abs`, the parameters are `int x`, and the return type is `int`. Recording only `Abs` would lose the currently visible type information, and would also leave later searches for the same or similar names without a specific location to return to. The method body is written here as `default`; the index treats it as part of the declaration text, and does not infer an execution path from it.

When reading onward from the type entry point, locate the target in this order: first confirm that the current namespace is still `ComputeSharp`, then confirm that the containing declaration block is `Hlsl`, and only then compare the parameters and return type of the target method. The benefit of this approach is that, even if the search results include the same short name, you can first use the type boundary to narrow the scope.

## Names Scattered Throughout the File

Line 741 is recorded as `Acos`. Nearby you can directly see:

```csharp
public static float Acos(float x) => default;
```

This entry and the earlier `Abs` should not be grouped into a single call record just because both are in `Hlsl`. The current record for `Acos` retains the `float` parameters and `float` return value; use this signature as the reference when looking it up. The distance from line 21 to line 741 only shows that they occupy different positions in the file, and is not evidence that they call each other.

No additional signature text is included on this page for the remaining anchors, and their names and locations are still recorded as-is:

| Name | Location | Use in the Index |

When you need to find `All` or `Any`, go directly to each name; do not assume that their parameters, return types or call order are the same just because the two names are adjacent. Likewise when you need to find `AsDouble`, first return to the declaration on line 2422, then continue from the actual text.

## Reading Approach After a Review

During review, the easiest mistake to overlook is conflating class names, method names and call sites. The records here have the following hierarchy:

- `ComputeSharp` is the namespace declared at the beginning of the file;
- `Hlsl` is the partial type on line 9;
- `Abs`,`Acos`,`All`,`Any`,`AsDouble` are the recorded method names distributed throughout that type;
- Line 21 and line 741 also retain complete method declarations that can be compared directly.

Therefore, if some code already explicitly specifies `Hlsl.Abs`, look it up by going to line 21 to check the declaration for the `int` version, rather than just searching globally for `Abs`. If all you know is the name `Acos`, first go to line 741 to check the `float` signature. For `All`,`Any` and `AsDouble`, this index first provides stable locations; the signature details should be read from the matching declarations before being added to the consumer records.

This index preserves the entry point and local symbol distribution of `Hlsl.g.cs` itself. # ComputeSharp Call Decision Note

`src/ComputeSharp/Graphics/Extensions/GraphicsDeviceExtensions.Resources.cs` is still a common entry point for locating the resource extension surface of ComputeSharp. Many people initially used this page as an index to the "start of the resource call chain"; it is retained because the entry is genuinely easy to find, but that description goes beyond what the file itself can support.

## The old note is retained

The provisional reading path in the initial draft was:

```text
GraphicsDeviceExtensions.Resources.cs
  -> Declaration in the file
  -> Direct references
  -> Code that calls this extension surface
```

When it was drawn with one-way arrows, the intent was to give someone seeing this file for the first time a sequence to follow. That note implicitly made two judgments: Resources could represent the scope of objects to trace; references leaving the extension file could be assembled into a stable call chain. After review, neither should be carried forward as a conclusion.

The file path can show that it is under `Graphics/Extensions`, and can narrow the reading starting point to `GraphicsDeviceExtensions.Resources.cs`; it cannot by itself determine whether resource objects have another entry path elsewhere, much less settle questions about resource lifetime, binding location, or memory ownership. The old diagram is not deleted, so that people who later encounter the old links do not assume these checks had already been completed at the time.

## How the reading changed in review

In this review, Resources in the filename was not treated as the name of a complete subsystem; it was used only as a search label. Once in the file, inspect the declaration itself first, then the types or members it directly touches. Only if either of those two places shows an explicit adjacency should we continue outward to callers. Directory hierarchy, similar names, and the word "resource" appearing in a caller no longer automatically count as the same relationship.

This change may look conservative, but it avoids a practical problem in the initial draft: when broadening the search starting from the directory, it is easy to misread "resource-related" as "initiated by this extension file." A file can provide an extension surface, but it is not necessarily where objects are created, stored, or released. The old index put all these actions behind the same arrow; it was quick to read, but tracing back through it puts the question at the wrong level.

When using this page now, use the following order:

```text
Path lookup
  -> Declaration in the current file
  -> Direct adjacency visible from the declaration
  -> Actual usage at specific callers
```

Step one only finds the file; it does not define behavior. Step two confirms which part of the extension surface is actually being examined; neighboring files in the same directory are not automatically included just because their names are similar. Step three records the relationships directly visible around the declaration, not the target implementation inferred from an impression of the module. Only in step four do we return to the callers: whether what appears there is a use result, parameter passing, or another forwarding layer must be judged separately at the call site.

This page does not list every caller. Such a list would quickly go stale after the initial draft and would turn the index into the sole record for maintaining resource relationships. What is retained here is the lookup order: first let the in-file declaration set the scope of the question, then let the actual call sites determine whether to continue tracing. If all someone wants to confirm is whether a given extension entry appears in this slice, stopping at step two is enough.

## About the old claim about "direct references"

The initial draft placed direct references and callers consecutively on a single line, so readers could easily see them as the same kind of relationship. After review, they should be treated separately. Types, members, or forwarding visible directly in the file are adjacencies at the current reading position; a caller, by contrast, is usage at another location. The former helps decide what to open next; only the latter may show what role a particular extension serves in actual code.

Therefore, when a resource name comes up, do not first infer where it leads from its name. First confirm whether it appears near the current declaration; if it does not, do not force a link to this index just to preserve the old diagram. This limitation does not say it is unrelated; it says this page has not recorded its relationship with this file.

## Boundary of the relationship with TerraFX

Call relationships involving TerraFX are documented separately in DOC-03. The two pages can link to each other, but the relationship diagram for DOC-03 should not be brought into this page: the starting point here is the extension file for ComputeSharp, while the other page handles another set of call adjacencies. When crossing over, first confirm in this file which declaration or direct reference is being traced, then continue at DOC-03; do not merge the two into one entry just because both questions touch resources or interop.

## What still applies

The earlier advice to "start with this file" remains useful, especially when the only two clues are Graphics and the resource extension. Its purpose is to shorten the initial lookup, not to replace subsequent judgment. The file name, directory, and extension surface can help someone get to the same code location; actual call relationships still need to be determined jointly from the area around the declaration and the specific use sites.

If someone later treats this as the current complete description of the relationships, they should see the correction above first. The old arrow can remain as the reading hint it was at the time, but it no longer means that starting from `GraphicsDeviceExtensions.Resources.cs` covers all resource-related paths.

This index wasn't organized by type name; it was anchored to a path first: `src/ComputeSharp.SourceGeneration.Hlsl/SyntaxRewriters/ShaderSourceRewriter.cs`. That label stayed in the page name afterward.

## Index Card

- Module: the existing C# module for ComputeSharp.
- Location: `src/ComputeSharp.SourceGeneration.Hlsl/SyntaxRewriters/ShaderSourceRewriter.cs`
- Entry point for this page: expand `SourceGeneration.Hlsl`, then open `SyntaxRewriters`.
- Adjacent record: DOC-08 is kept as another note for the shared entry point.

There was no symbol table here originally. The reading notes only called for finding the file, its parent directory, and names in the same directory, then lining them up. For the investigation at the time, this was faster than searching the whole repository first; after jumping from the index into the file, readers would decide whether to keep looking outside the directory. So in this old record, "call index" referred to both a path index and a reading order, without a strict distinction between them.

## Old Arrows Left in Place

```text
ComputeSharp
  │
  └─ SourceGeneration.Hlsl
       │
       └─ SyntaxRewriters
            │
            └─ ShaderSourceRewriter.cs
                 │
                 └─ Shared entry point record (DOC-08)
```

The arrows were originally drawn to show call direction. In the actual record, they only connect a point reached during a code-reading session to the next local reference; calling them call relationships later made this page easy to misread. The diagram was left in place during review because existing reading notes still marked file locations in this order. DOC-08 below the diagram is not a runtime jump either; it is just navigation added at the time to put the two entry points together.

## Reading Approach at the Time

After opening the file, first check whether its directory still retains the `SyntaxRewriters` level; if the directory structure is unchanged, keep using the "source-rewriting entry point" label. The index treated `ShaderSource` in the filename as a clue near the HLSL source output, so subsequent reading often started with this file rather than tracing back from a caller or the generated output first.

This order was retained as a working habit:

1. Locate `SyntaxRewriters` under `SourceGeneration.Hlsl`.
2. Open `ShaderSourceRewriter.cs` and record the local objects you see on this pass in your reading notes.
3. If the issue is on the shared entry point side, consult DOC-08 next.

There was no fixed format for the second step. Some people recorded only the filename, while others added a line about the directory relationships; the index itself did not collect the members seen on each reading pass, nor did it produce a call table for side-by-side comparison. Grouping these scattered annotations under the name "call index" early on made it easy for readers to assume that all relationships into and out of the file had already been listed here.

## Review Notes

The later review added back just one fact that was easy to lose sight of: this page points to an entry point in the baseline source, not the location of a newly added implementation. Earlier notes put heavy emphasis on "entry point," as though all related reading should start here; this was not an enumeration of an actual call chain. Even so, the original index was neither renamed nor reordered. Existing references still use this path to find points for cross-checking historical behavior.

The review retained the old recommendation to "start with this file." It is still useful for browsing directories, but should not be read as a claim about the complete call path. The old diagram was kept for the same reason: it records the reading habits at the time and why `ShaderSourceRewriter.cs` was included in the index, not a breakdown of the file's internal responsibilities.

## Index Endnote

If all you need is the old reading entry point related to HLSL, the path is direct enough; if you need to trace why a particular rewrite happened, this index page does not go that far. The plan was to add specific objects to the original record after reading the file, but that was never completed. DOC-08 only provides navigation to the shared entry point; it cannot replace the missing index of the file's internals here.

This page retains the old name and arrows to make it easier to check what the word "call" actually covered in earlier notes.

versions.body:
# Input Type Memory Decision Record

Input types cannot be inferred from a particular resource binding. A binding records which resources are placed into slots at runtime; input types record which types the shader declarations require those slots to have. In simple examples, the two often appear together and are easily mistaken for the same table.

For this round, query responsibility stays on the pixel shader side. When callers need to interpret input slots, they should get type descriptions from the public query, not reconstruct a type table from effect registration data, the current resource set, or their own caches. This only draws a line between declarations and bindings; it does not mean that all other descriptor outputs belong in the same entry point.

There were two alternatives at the time.

- The type table could be assembled on read; as long as the element contents were the same, how it was stored would not need to be exposed.
- The type table should be part of the generated result; callers should not each store and interpret slot information themselves.

The latter direction was provisionally adopted, but no guarantee was made about the underlying storage relationships. The material available at the time only supported "input types should be obtained from the declaration side"; it was not enough to determine whether repeated reads refer to the same storage, or how results from different shaders are isolated.

Standalone shader source was left as a related issue. It shares context with descriptor-lifecycle, but there was no material at the time showing that source output should be delivered along with input types. Source must not be put into the type query's return object just because both relate to generated results.

Additional note: input slot order should be interpreted according to the declarations, not the order in which resources are actually bound. Updating resources, missing resources, or replacing the resource set should not change the meaning of the type description.

To confirm later:

1. What memory relationship callers need to observe across repeated reads.
2. Whether shaders with no inputs still use the same query entry point.
3. Which output object should provide standalone shader source.

# Input Type Memory Decision Record

The earliest record framed the issue as "whether to compute the type table on demand." On review, that framing was too close to implementation details. What callers actually depend on is the interpretation of input declarations, not how many construction steps happen internally during a particular read.

## Earlier position retained

The initial position was not to let callers infer input types from current resource bindings. That position has not changed. Bindings are runtime state; input types belong to the shader's declared inputs. The former change as resources are updated; the latter should not be treated as a list that changes with runtime conditions.

An early note stated:

> The type table can be computed on the fly as needed; as long as the contents are the same, callers do not need to know how it is stored.

This sentence is retained as the working assumption at the time. It made no promise that every read would create new data, nor that different reads would necessarily share the same underlying storage. The problem with the original wording is that "the contents are the same" only says that the element values appear identical; it says nothing about the object relationships callers see when they repeatedly retrieve descriptions.

## Objects distinguished during review

The review did not call for all descriptor data to be combined into one large object. Instead, it first distinguished several kinds of information that are easy to conflate.

Input type descriptions specify the declared types of input slots. Resource texture descriptions describe the resource side. Numeric metadata has its own established uses. They may be adjacent during generation, but that does not make them data that callers Fang Ke can use interchangeably.

This means effect registration XML cannot be described as a fallback protocol for input type queries. Registration data can provide the information needed for effect registration, but that does not make it a source from which arbitrary callers can reconstruct input slot types. If callers infer types from XML, declarations, registration text, and runtime bindings will become entangled again.

Likewise, whether resources have been bound should not determine whether an input type description exists. An unbound state, resource updates, or running with a different set of resources are all resource-side states; they cannot rewrite shader declarations into a new type table.

## Proposals retained but not adopted

Someone proposed at the time that, for easier debugging, a larger descriptor snapshot could be generated containing input types, resource descriptions, and source, with callers taking what they need. That approach was not adopted.

Its apparent benefit was fewer entry points, but it did not actually answer three questions: whether source should be exposed in the first place, at what point resource descriptions are valid, and whether callers can retain the snapshot. Forcing different behaviors into one container would only give input type queries responsibilities that had not yet been confirmed.

The following original suggestion is therefore kept on record, but should not be reinstated:

> If it is unclear where source belongs, it can temporarily be attached alongside the input type result, so callers can pick it up as they read the descriptor.

That suggestion has been discarded. The input type entry point describes declared input slots; it is not a transport channel for arbitrary generated output. If source were returned alongside it, callers would naturally infer that the two have the same lifetime and visibility; the available material does not support that inference.

A more moderate suggestion was to reassemble an identical type result on every read. That suggestion did not become a decision either. Identical element values do not rule out repeated-read costs, nor do they explain the relationship between a stable description and a temporary copy. It can only be retained as an implementation option, not used as a description of public behavior.

## Boundaries for this version

This version of the page makes only the following decisions.

Input type queries concern declarations, not the set of resources currently bound. The type result needs to express the slot order in the declaration. Callers should not reconstruct this result from XML, resource texture descriptions, or bound resources.

A memory view is the direction for further review, but this version does not refine "view" into a complete set of requirements for repeated reads, shared storage, or the generator's allocation strategy. Any old record saying "identical contents are enough" can only be read as discussion that had not yet been settled, not as an interface promise.

Standalone shader source remains a separate topic. The ability to query input types does not automatically make it part of the same query result. Any later discussion of source output should first identify its actual caller-facing output location, then decide how it relates to the writer, cache, or other generated data.

## Open questions

- Whether empty inputs are represented using the same read mechanism as ordinary inputs.
- Whether callers might mistake resource texture descriptions for a source of input types.
- If source output is exposed separately, whether its responsibilities and scope of visibility need a separate description.

This version does not settle all of these questions. What has been decided is that input types are not reconstructed from runtime bindings or registration text; standalone shader source is not delivered as an add-on through the input type entry point.

# Input Type Memory Decision Record

This record does not trace a single continuous implementation thread, but rather several rounds of mistakenly grouping adjacent objects together and then gradually separating them. Input types, resource descriptions, registration data, and standalone shader source were all once folded into the same notion of "descriptor output". The decision that eventually remained was much narrower than that notion: establish only what input type queries themselves are responsible for, without deciding in advance for other output objects.

The current entry point for reviewing this is still `src/ComputeSharp.D2D1/Shaders/Interop/D2D1PixelShaderEffect.cs`. This path is enough to bring the input type topic close to the existing code, but it does not establish ownership of writer, cache, effect registration XML, or all descriptor data. Follow-up checks for input types are retained in CSH-201; the investigation into responsibility for standalone shader source continues in CSH-217.

## 2023-04-19: Scope of the Initial Record

The first version addressed only one distinction that examples can easily obscure: input declarations and resource bindings are not the same thing. A binding describes which resource goes into which slot at a particular moment at runtime; an input type describes the slot type that the shader requires in its declaration. When a simple effect shows both at the same time, callers can easily mistake binding order for type table order.

The choice made at the time was not to have callers reconstruct input types from the current binding state. Public queries should be handled on the pixel shader side, and callers should not infer slot types from a resource collection, effect registration data, or an array they maintain themselves. This decision did not require other descriptor outputs to use the same entry point, nor did it require source and type descriptions to appear together.

The initial text abbreviated "declaration order" as "type table order". This wording left room for ambiguity: some would interpret it as the runtime ordering of resources, while others would interpret it as the internal collection order during generation. There was not enough material at the time to address more detailed memory relationships, so the only option was to first separate the objects being queried from the objects being bound.

A working assumption was also recorded during the same period:

> The type table can be computed temporarily on demand; as long as its contents are the same, callers do not need to know how it is stored.

This is not the current requirement. It reflects the fact that, at the time, the only concern was whether element values could be read, and repeated reads, storage relationships, and generation paths had not yet been included in the interface discussion. The original wording is preserved because the subsequent corrections began precisely with "identical contents are not enough".

standalone shader source was initially only an adjacency issue. Like input types, it fell within the scope of the discussion in descriptor-lifecycle, but there was no evidence that callers should obtain source through the input-type query. It was deliberately not written as a requirement early on, to avoid disguising an unconfirmed source output as an existing type-query capability.

## 2024-03-07: Review addendum separated the objects

The second pass did not expand the scope of API, but separated several objects that were often conflated into a single table.

Input type descriptions explain declared inputs. Resource texture descriptions explain information on the resource side. numeric descriptor metadata retains its own purpose. They may be adjacent to one another during generation, but that does not mean they have the same caller-facing semantics.

This separation first ruled out the idea of "inferring types from effect registration XML." XML can participate in effect registration, but that does not automatically make it responsible for input-type queries. If callers were asked to infer input types from registration text, registration data, string representations, and shader declarations would once again be bound together; the fact that data appears somewhere does not mean that location is the public query protocol.

The second result was that resource bindings cannot change the meaning of type descriptions. Whether a resource has not yet been bound, a resource has been updated, or the same declaration is used by another batch of resources, these are all runtime states. They can change which resources the effect sees at a given moment, but they cannot rewrite the input declaration as another type list.

At the time, the review compressed this idea into the phrase "read by declaration, not by binding." This phrase can still help distinguish the objects, but it is insufficient to explain the memory relationship of repeated queries, and it is also insufficient to specify what kind of returned object the caller will receive. Therefore, it should not be copied alone as a complete interface specification.

## 2024-03-08: Large snapshot that was never implemented

After the review, an apparently simpler proposal emerged: generate a relatively large descriptor snapshot for debugging, containing input types, resource descriptions, and source at the same time, and let callers find the needed part in the snapshot themselves.

This proposal did not pass. It did not answer whether source should be made public; it did not answer at which points resource descriptions are valid; and it did not answer whether callers can retain, cache, or reuse this snapshot across different reads. Putting three different objects into one container only obscures their respective responsibility boundaries.

The recommendation left at the time was as follows:

> When the location of standalone shader source is not yet clear, it can be attached alongside the input type results; the caller already has the descriptor data and can simply read the source as well.

**Deprecated.** The role of the input type entry point is to describe declared input slots, not to relay all generated outputs. Attaching source alongside the results would imply that source has the same lifetime and visibility as the type results, which was precisely what had not been confirmed at the time.

Another suggestion that was not adopted was to rebuild a type result with the same elements on every read. Its scope is narrower than a large snapshot, but it still cannot serve as a public description. Having the same elements does not establish the cost of each read, the relationships between objects, or whether the underlying generated data is stable. This suggestion only shows that someone at the time was trying to sidestep the storage issue, not that the interface already allowed it to be ignored.

## Old examples: three misinterpretations that once worked

These old examples are retained not to offer callers alternative approaches, but to highlight three recurring points of confusion.

**Old example A: read the registration data first, then guess the input types.**

This example treated effect registration XML as a type query protocol. It once explained a small number of examples, because the registration data and shader declarations both appeared in connection with the same effect. But it did not explain the relationship between results across repeated reads, nor whether callers should directly use the information appearing in XML. Not currently adopted.

**Old example B: list types based on currently bound resources.**

This example treated the set of already bound resources as the source of the type table. It looked reasonable in a runtime environment with all resources present, but could not account for unbound resources, resource updates, or the same declaration in different runtime environments. More fundamentally, it incorrectly presented runtime ordering as declared input order. Not currently adopted.

**Old example C: include source as an additional field in the type results.**

This example never became a stable approach; it was only an idea for debugging convenience: since the caller had already read the type information, it seemed they could also obtain the shader source. It did not clarify responsibility for source output, nor did it explain how the writer, cache, or caller's results should fit together. Not currently adopted.

These three old examples mistook registration data, binding state, and adjacent generated output, respectively, for the input type query itself. Keeping these examples is more useful than leaving only "do not mix them," because the same shortcuts may be encountered again during maintenance.

## 2025-09-09: counterexamples shifted the focus of the discussion

CSH-201 later added a counterexample. I will not repeat the individual case from the card here; I will only record the changes in judgment it brought: deriving the input type from the current binding is insufficient. After the counterexample appeared, the early claim that "identical content is enough" lost its footing, because it did not explain whether the identical content came from a fixed declaration or from a runtime state that can change.

This change did not prove that all generated data should use the same memory-management approach. It only forced the semantics of the input-type query itself to become explicit. bytecode, source output, packing, registration data, and resource descriptions remain adjacent objects; whether they are cached, whether they share storage, or whether they have a public entry point cannot be inferred from this one counterexample.

Subsequently, CSH-201 entered the processing state. This only indicates that the input-type thread needs continued checking; it must not be read as meaning that implementation is complete, nor as meaning that all descriptor outputs have been given conclusions of equal standing. The card's role here is to preserve an investigation entry point, not to replace the decision on this page.

After the counterexample, one brief reminder in the review was: first separate "declaration order" from "binding order" before discussing output form. This sequence is worth preserving. If the meaning of the result sequence has not yet been determined, discussing whether to reuse memory or cache is effectively optimizing a table that has not been defined.

## 2025-10-15: the source track did not close as a result

CSH-217's topic remains an investigation into who is responsible for the existing behavior of standalone shader, not an acceptance item for input-type functionality. The public note left at the time was: one point in standalone shader source remained unconfirmed; the card lacked specific inputs, so it would not enter implementation for now.

That record supports only one limited conclusion: the source track had not been closed out at that time. It cannot prove that source already had a particular return value, nor that writer, cache, or generator had already selected a particular output format. Writing a postponement opinion as a complete design decision would recreate the illusion that input types and source were handled by the same entry point.

The next day's blocking reason should likewise be understood at its original scale: the test machine used by source generator, writer, and cache pipeline was occupied by another regression. This explains why the investigation stopped; it does not indicate that any of the components above was modified, still less that standalone shader source should be exposed by any particular layer.

Therefore, bringing the input-type workstream to closure does not automatically decide the source question. The two tracks share the same lifecycle discussion, but not the same public-facing responsibility: one explains the type description of input declarations; the other still needs to be checked against the actual location of source output.

## Review excerpts and overturned attribution

One review note framed the question as: "If the caller can see type memory, should it naturally also be able to see source?" This premise was not accepted. type memory is a read-only result for input slot types; source is a separate output object. Both may help with debugging, but "both are useful for debugging" is not a reason to combine them into a single API.

Another note came closer to the boundary that was eventually adopted: "Do not infer public responsibilities from similarly named generation stages." It was used to address the adjacency of input description memory, embedded bytecode memory, and standalone shader source. This reminder was not saying that these objects were unrelated; rather, it required first identifying what each item meant to callers, before discussing whether navigation between adjacent items was needed.

For a time, the problem was attributed to effect registration XML lacking enough fields. This attribution was later overturned. Even if XML listed more information, it still would not address the need for input types to be declaration-oriented and express declared input order, or the question of how to describe memory relationships across repeated reads. The fact that the registration path owns the text does not mean that the text inherently becomes a result of the caller's API.

Attributing the problem to insufficient resource texture descriptions does not hold up either. Resource descriptions can help explain the resource-side composition, but cannot replace declared input types. These two kinds of information are especially prone to misuse when they are adjacent; the decision on this page is to prevent callers from treating one as the source of the other.

## 2026-02-03: Current decision

Following the preceding records, reviews, counterexamples, and revisions to the old approach, the behavior of input type queries is fixed as follows:

D2D1PixelShader.GetInputTypes<T>() returns ReadOnlyMemory<D2D1PixelShaderInputType>, preserves declared input order, and reuses one generated memory manager across lookups.

This requirement addresses only input type queries. It does not announce that source output is available, nor does it change the status of standalone shader source, which is still pending confirmation. Call Fang Ke to understand the input type as a read-only in-memory result in declaration order; it should no longer be interpreted as a collection that varies with bindings, data reconstructed from XML, or a generic descriptor snapshot containing source.

The part concerning repeated queries is precisely an explicit correction to the earlier claim of "compute temporarily on demand." The old wording cared only whether the same elements could be obtained each time; the current requirement fixes the memory relationship of generated results across repeated lookups. This correction does not authorize the caller to write to or take control of that memory; it only rules out describing each read as creating an unrelated temporary type table.

The part about ordering is also not a suggestion that can be overridden by the current resource bindings. The result sequence is anchored to the shader declaration. If the caller needs to interpret the current resources, it should use the appropriate resource-binding or resource-description path, and should no longer mix runtime state back into the ordering of the input type.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "declared inputs" as Declared
    state "input type lookup" as Lookup
    state "repeated lookup" as Repeated
    state "standalone shader source" as Source
    state "unconfirmed" as Pending
    [*] --> Declared
    Declared --> Lookup
    Lookup --> Repeated
    Repeated --> [*]
    [*] --> Source
    Source --> Pending
```

The two lines in the diagram represent only the objects that have already been separated: the declaration feeds into the input type query, and the query permits repeated reads; standalone shader source remains unconfirmed. The diagram does not indicate that source has gained a new return entry point, nor that source and the input type result share a lifecycle.

## Adjacent issues not yet separated out

The CSH-217 matter still requires concrete input before proceeding. What the existing record can confirm is that the investigation has been deferred, not that source behavior has been superseded by the input-type decision. If a public entry point for standalone shader source is confirmed later, its relationship with the writer, cache, and caller results should be described separately, and only then should we decide whether this page needs a navigation link to it.

One smaller issue remains here: whether a shader with no inputs expresses an empty result through the same query entry point. It does not change the current decision, because the current decision concerns the type, order, and repeated-read relationship of query results; however, caller examples may still need to specify how to read the result for empty input. This issue cannot be resolved by treating resource bindings as a special source.

If a large descriptor snapshot is proposed again later to support debugging, first answer whether source is visible, when resource descriptions become valid, and whether input types still preserve declaration order. Without these answers, the snapshot merely recombines objects that have already been separated.

## Appendix of old examples

The three earlier examples—inferring types from XML, listing types according to the current bindings, and placing source alongside the type result—remain archived. They should not be restored to the caller documentation, but they illustrate why the current boundary exists: registration data is not a public query; binding state is not a declaration; adjacent generated output is not the same return object.

This page only establishes the input-type track. standalone shader source remains under investigation along CSH-217, and should not gain any additional commitments based on the already established input-type behavior.

title: Input Descriptor Memory Trial Proposal

versions.body:
# Input Descriptor Memory Trial Proposal

This trial starts by separating input descriptors from CPU execution diagnostics. The former concerns how much information the caller can still retain after receiving the descriptor; the latter concerns what clues should be left when the CPU path fails. Putting the two in the same interface would lead callers to mistake diagnostic data for part of the descriptor.

There are two candidate approaches for the input descriptor: rebuild it on every request, or hand over the prepared content as read-only memory. The former is straightforward to implement, but repeated requests for the same shader repeat the same work; the latter requires an upfront agreement that callers must not treat the returned content as a writable buffer. The initial draft leans toward the second, but it has not yet decided which layer should prepare the indices, filtering method, and level-of-detail information in the descriptor.

CPU execution diagnostics will initially stay out of the input descriptor's return value. The trial only requires successful and failed calls to each leave separately inspectable records, so that the input state does not later have to be inferred solely from exception paths.

If a call changes the contents of the read-only memory, or if the diagnostic record depends on the caller guessing internal state, withdraw this combined approach and provide separate descriptor-query and diagnostic entry points.

# Input Descriptor Memory Trial Proposal

The initial draft discussed input descriptor memory and CPU execution diagnostics together because both appear in caller troubleshooting. After review, it keeps this shared entry point but no longer treats them as the same data: the descriptor answers "what is the input," while diagnostics answer "where did CPU execution diverge."

When reviewing `src/ComputeSharp.D2D1/Shaders/Interop/D2D1PixelShaderEffect.cs`, the focus should be on the interop boundary of the D2D1 pixel shader, rather than treating this path as the implementation domain for all descriptors. The current proposal covers only input descriptor queries for this object; embedded bytecode, effect XML and binding slots are outside this trial.

## Input Descriptor

Candidate A generates a new array at request time. It is easy to reason about, but every query allocates again, so repeated reads of the same shader provide no benefit. Candidate B prepares it once and returns it as read-only memory. It preserves the convenience of sequential reads and also allows the caller Fang Ke to pass the descriptor to read-only checking logic.

The review retained two constraints on Candidate B. First, the order of the returned content must still correspond to the declared input indices; caching must not change the order visible to the caller. Second, the filtering method and level-of-detail metadata must be retained along with the descriptor; the implementation must not leave only texture positions for the caller to fill in by guessing. Whether the underlying storage is reused still needs to be confirmed by actual call results; the trial interface does not promise that the caller Fang Ke will hold a writable array.

## Records for the CPU Path

Diagnostics are not attached to descriptor elements. A successful call should leave a record that this execution passed through the CPU path; a failed call should retain enough clues to distinguish input descriptor reading from the execution process. The cost is that the caller must check two locations, but this avoids disguising an execution error as a missing input descriptor.

The earlier proposal to "return diagnostics and the descriptor together" is no longer adopted. If it is later found that the caller can locate the CPU execution problem only through the descriptor, reassess whether to add a correlation marker; until then, do not expand the return object.

The conditions for withdrawing this approach remain specific: if reused memory makes the indices, filtering method, or level-of-detail metadata inconsistent with the declaration, revert to per-request generation; if diagnostics cannot distinguish successful from failed calls, suspend this diagnostic entry point and do not fill the gap with an ambiguous state.

# Input Description Memory Trial Plan

The original problem was not a missing descriptor name, but that callers could not tell whether the content they held after reading the input still retained the details from its declaration. The first draft therefore pursued "returning memory" and "CPU execution diagnostics" in parallel. The flaw in that version was treating troubleshooting convenience as a data model: putting diagnostics into descriptor queries would naturally lead callers to rely on the description results to explain execution failures.

A later review brought the discussion back to the interop object at `src/ComputeSharp.D2D1/Shaders/Interop/D2D1PixelShaderEffect.cs`. The decision here is the shape of the input description query, not a reorganization of the entire shader execution chain. The path remains a starting point for verification; it does not replace checking actual call results.

## The Two Retained Options

Generating an array for each query still has one advantage: each query can rebuild the descriptions from the declarations as they stand at that point, without having to explain the lifetime of reused storage. But it turns repeated queries into repeated allocations and can easily lead callers to think they own the returned array. The other option is to expose the prepared descriptions as read-only memory. This suits consecutive reads and also forces the interface to distinguish between "readable" and "modifiable."

The review rejected a compromise: reusing the internal content while suggesting in the documentation that callers use Fang Ke to modify it and then pass it back. That would make descriptor queries responsible for an update protocol, while the object in this change only handles queries. Input indices, filters, and level-of-detail metadata should be preserved as part of the descriptions; they cannot be re-derived on the caller side.

## Current Trial Criteria

Following this review, check the input description interface against the following behavior:

D2D1PixelShader.GetInputDescriptions<T>() returns ReadOnlyMemory<D2D1InputDescription> with the declared indices, filters, and level-of-detail metadata, backed by a reusable array.

This means the first draft's "possibly generating a new array every time" is no longer the default direction. The reusable array supports query results; it does not become a buffer managed through calls to Fang Ke. During the trial, examine one successful call and one failed call separately: the former confirms that the descriptions read still match the declarations, and the latter confirms that failure has not caused the descriptions themselves to be rewritten or replaced with execution information.

## Diagnostics Are Not Part of the Return Value

CPU execution diagnostics will continue to be handled as an adjacent issue. They need to let investigators distinguish between "the description query completed" and "CPU execution failed," but do not require adding diagnostic fields to every `D2D1InputDescription`. This adds another place to look, in exchange for descriptor results that can remain stable without changing meaning based on the state of a particular execution.

The earlier proposal to bundle the two types of information in the return value has been dropped. That proposal would work for a one-off troubleshooting example, but would lead long-term callers to mistakenly cache execution state. If the two do need to be linked in the future, prefer adding a marker on the diagnostic side that points back to the query; do not expand the input description elements.

## Boundaries Still to Be Tested

The trial is not intended to verify all D2D1 behavior, but two specific branches. The first is whether, across consecutive queries of the same shader, the reused array still preserves the declared index order, filters, and level-of-detail metadata. The second is whether success and failure records for the CPU path can be inspected separately without reading or modifying descriptor contents.

If the first branch shows inconsistent content, roll back array reuse and return to the approach of rebuilding descriptions on each query; if checking the second branch requires guessing at the input descriptions, pause the diagnostic entry point trial and do not put uncertain state back into the query results. Related investigation material can be compared alongside the DOC-13 concurrent registration issue, but this discussion does not extend to registration boundaries.

title: Resource Texture Description Troubleshooting Tree

versions.body:
# Resource Texture Description Troubleshooting Tree

First, record resource texture descriptions and concurrent registration separately. They may both be mentioned in the same round, but there was no evidence at the time that either caused the other.

```text
Description anomaly observed
|
+-- Difference already present before the call?
|   +-- Yes: record the input description and stop determining the source
|   `-- No or unknown: record the observation after the call
|
`-- Concurrent registration also appears?
    +-- Yes: open a separate registration record
    `-- No: retain the description sample
```

The early practice was to handle any observed description change as concurrent registration first. This entry only indicates what was checked first during the investigation; it cannot establish that the description set came from registration, and it does not distinguish between the input before the call and the result after the call.

The description record must retain at least three things: what was seen before the call, the call site that triggered the observation, and what was directly seen after the call. If it already differed before the call, do not write the current call down as the source; if the change appeared only after the call, do not immediately write that it was caused by registration.

Tracing old issue names and call names leads back to `src/ComputeSharp.D2D1.SourceGenerators/Diagnostics/DiagnosticDescriptors.cs`. Verify the diagnostic object and name here first. If only the declaration is visible, record "name verified" and stop there; do not infer ownership of resource texture descriptions or registration handling from the file location.

Stop conditions: when before-and-after-call states are unavailable, retain the observation as incomplete; when there are only registration-side clues, still save the description sample separately; when neither side has direct state, do not fill in a cause.

Open item: In the report, does "order change" refer to declaration indices, description ordering, or different observation locations?

# Resource Texture Description Troubleshooting Tree

The earliest page put changes to resource texture descriptions and concurrent registration under the same entry point. That interpretation was carried forward because the two terms often appeared in the same round of investigation; it did not prove that they were causally related. The second pass kept the old entry point but split the description side from the registration side, making it easier to see exactly which part of the state was missing from the original record.

## Keep the old tree

```text
Old entry point (retained; cannot close out on its own)
|
+-- Description appears different
|   +-- Someone is checking concurrent registration: check registration first
|   `-- No one is checking it: record the description first
|
`-- No change observed
    `-- Previously, this would switch to checking registration
```

The last branch of this tree is no longer suitable as a conclusion. Not seeing a change only means that this observation did not show any additional change; it does not mean that registration did not occur, or that registration should explain the description. The old tree remains here because early records only went this far; removing it would make those short records lose their original entry point.

The old rule was, "If the description result shows an additional change, first ask whether there was concurrent registration." It lets the investigation start in one direction, but misses an earlier input issue: the difference may already have existed before the call. When the pre-call state was not captured, do not fill the gap with the familiar term registration.

## Record before-and-after snippets on the description side

At minimum, a review should try to fill in three points: what was visible before the call, which call triggered the observation, and what was directly visible after the call. The record can still be kept if all three are not available, but any missing item must be left in the record and not replaced with speculation.

When a difference already existed before the call, the current call is not the only possible source of what was observed. First record the input description and observation location; stop making the judgment "the current call introduced the change." If an addition, omission, or ordering change appears after the call, record the observation only as post-call; if there is no direct state after registration processing, still do not attribute it to registration.

"Description is wrong" is too broad; during review, check which of these the report actually points to:

- Element contents differ;
- Count differs;
- Order differs;
- The location where the result was observed differs;
- There is only a verbal summary, with no sample.

"Order changed" cannot directly be treated as a change in declaration indices. It may simply be that the two observations were presented differently. Without a pre-call sample, retaining "unconfirmed" is more accurate than choosing an explanation.

```text
Description side
|
+-- Pre-call state recorded?
|   +-- Yes: compare before and after; write the change category
|   `-- No: mark the gap; stop source attribution
|
+-- Additional change after the call?
|   +-- Yes: retain the sample and observation location
|   `-- No: leave the observation blank
|
`-- Direct state on the registration side?
    +-- Yes: record separately and compare the order
    `-- No: end the description branch
```

The direct state here is not the issue title, an old TODO, or a topic someone else is investigating. It must be linkable to the state directly after registration processing for this case. Without this layer, the description side cannot automatically be upgraded to a concurrent registration issue.

## Trace back from the diagnostic name

Old troubleshooting notes are routed by issue name and call name to `src/ComputeSharp.D2D1.SourceGenerators/Diagnostics/DiagnosticDescriptors.cs`. This entry point is useful for verifying the diagnostic object and adjacent declarations, but the source of the description set cannot be determined from the filename alone, nor can declaration order be used to infer runtime order.

One attempt estimated the description-processing order from the relative order of the diagnostic names, then used that estimate to explain concurrent registration. No link from declarations to runtime state was found, so the attempt stopped. The file can still be used to confirm the names in the old notes; if opening it shows only diagnostic declarations, the record should stop at "diagnostic name verified"; do not write the declaration entry point as the processing entry point.

## Counterexample left after review

A description sample can have no confirmable registration anomaly. This counterexample is sufficient only to refute "any description change must necessarily be accompanied by registration"; it does not explain why the description differs, or show that all samples with no observed registration came from the same path.

So the description record should first complete its own before-and-after state; the registration record should then cover the post-processing state. If the registration observation came before the description call, do not turn around and use the description call to explain the registration; if the description call came before the registration observation, do not therefore say that the description triggered registration. When their order cannot be compared, record them as parallel observations.

Still unresolved is what the "ordering change" refers to: the earlier page did not settle which one of the pre-call sample, post-call sample, observation location, and comparison object needs to be added.

# Resource Texture Descriptor Troubleshooting Tree

This page did not start with a conclusion. At first, someone noted only two terms that appeared next to each other in the observed situation, and only later were the input, post-call observations, diagnostic names, and registration state gradually separated into several lines of inquiry. The old passages are still retained because later readers often arrive via one of these terms; but the old assessments have already been marked where they appear and should not be treated directly as the current starting point.

## 2023-03-20: Two terms were initially grouped together

The only initial observations were that the resource texture descriptor looked different and that someone mentioned concurrent registration in the same round. There were no complete snippets from before and after the call, nor any direct state information connecting registration handling with the descriptor result. So a very rough tree was recorded at the time:

```text
An anomaly appears in the report
|
+-- Concerns a descriptor change
|   +-- Registration lead in the same round: check registration first
|   `-- No registration lead: record the descriptor for now
|
`-- No additional changes
    `-- Wait for the next observation
```

This tree addressed only the question of where to start a record. It gave short messages at least a direction to follow, but did not clarify whether the descriptor was an input, a result, or simply an observed state. In practice, records often retained only one half, either "the descriptor is wrong" or "someone is investigating registration", forcing the next reader to guess what had been seen at the time.

The old rule in the initial draft was as follows and has been retired:

> Once the descriptor changes, prioritize investigating concurrent registration.

There was a practical reason for it at the time: registration was a term people brought up more readily, and everyone wanted to narrow the scope by first following a familiar direction. But that reason does not establish causation. A descriptor difference may have already existed before the call, or it may only have been noticed for the first time after the call. The old rule did not distinguish between these two cases, so it can serve only as a historical starting point, not as an endpoint for troubleshooting.

An early note also said, "If it does not reproduce, keep a sample and do not fill in a cause." Brief as this sentence was, it was still safer than inventing a cause. Later, it became clear that the samples themselves were not specific enough either: if a sample said only "descriptor anomaly", it was impossible to tell later whether the input and result had ever been compared. Retaining the instruction to stop and adding detail to the sample were the focus of the first revision.

## Three fields left alongside the review

The first review did not delete the rough tree, but added three pieces of information to look for beside it: the descriptor visible before the call, the call site that triggered the observation, and changes that could be directly confirmed after the call. If one field is missing, the record can still be kept, but the gap must be visible and must not be filled by inference from the other two fields.

This changed the order of the questions. The old starting point first asked "Was there any parallel registration"; after the added notes, the first question became "Was it already different before the call". If differences already existed before the call, the current call cannot be recorded as their sole source. In that case, retain the input descriptor and the observation location, then stop making judgments about the source. Additions, omissions, or ordering changes after the call only prove that the observation occurred after the call, and cannot be attributed to the current call based on timing alone.

The intended meaning of the review margin note was:

> First clearly document the descriptor's before-and-after states; registration has its own state and cannot supply causality for the descriptor side.

This does not mean reconstructing the entire execution process every time. It only restricts one common way of writing things up: recording the presence of registration-side activity as the cause on the descriptor side because someone was also investigating registration in the same round. The two things can happen at the same time, or they can simply be separate issues.

If the pre-call state was not retained, the safest record is "Cannot distinguish differences already present in the input from differences after the call". If all you have is a post-call impression, you also cannot project it back into a pre-call fact. If even the call site itself is unclear, the descriptor-side record can only retain the problem terms and the places where information still needs to be added; it cannot fill those gaps with diagnostic names or the registration line of inquiry.

## Operational margin notes from the earlier investigation

The early margin notes also contained a more abbreviated rule of thumb: "When you see a descriptor change, look for a race first." It had the same bias as the first version of the tree, but left no explanation of why this should be done. Looking back at the actual records later, this rule of thumb would obscure at least two distinct gaps: one where there was no pre-call sample at all, and another where differences already existed before the call but the observer first noticed them after the call.

Therefore, a report of "no change" also does not justify going straight to checking for races. No additional visible change may mean that this observation did not capture the change, or it may mean that the input and result were the same. It is neither positive evidence that registration occurred nor proof that descriptor-side issues have been ruled out. The old margin note is retained, with "no longer applicable later on" written beside it, because old records may still have been saved according to this rule of thumb.

```text
Old report says only "no change"
|
+-- Is a pre-call sample available?
|   +-- Yes: compare before and after, and record the result
|   `-- No: retain the empty observation
|
`-- Is there a direct state from after registration processing?
    +-- Yes: put it in the registration-side record
    `-- No: do not choose an explanation
```

The "direct state" here must be linked to that particular instance of registration processing. An issue title, a secondhand account of an old to-do item, or someone saying they are investigating registration is not enough. Without a post-processing state, the registration line of inquiry cannot be elevated to an observed registration anomaly; likewise, without before-and-after descriptor snippets, the descriptor line of inquiry cannot be elevated to a change caused by the call.

## 2024-03-06: Following diagnostic names for a while

During the second pass at organizing the material, the old issue name and call name led the investigation back to `src/ComputeSharp.D2D1.SourceGenerators/Diagnostics/DiagnosticDescriptors.cs`. This file is still a useful navigation entry point, but its purpose is narrower than was imagined at the time: it can help verify diagnostic objects, names, and nearby declarations, but the path alone cannot prove that resource texture descriptor handling or registration processing is implemented here.

At the time, an attempt was made to infer the descriptor processing order from the order of adjacent diagnostic names, and then use that order to explain concurrent registration. This attempt found no direct connection from the declarations to runtime state, so it stopped at the declaration layer. The failure was not that this file had no value, but that the adjacent positions of declarations were treated as an execution order.

Only two kinds of results should be retained when tracing back: whether the old diagnostic names match the declarations, and whether the trace stopped at the declarations or went on to find references. If all you see after opening the file are diagnostic objects, simply write "names verified". Do not record the Diagnostics directory as the location where resource texture descriptors are processed, or infer the order of descriptor results from a group of adjacent declarations.

The old plan once read:

> After finding DiagnosticDescriptors.cs, the descriptor order can be determined from the name order alone.

This passage is now explicitly marked as subsequently overturned, but it is not being deleted. It explains why some older records used "the diagnostic name at the same location" as a basis. Following this path can now only confirm the name and the declaration entry point; whether it actually reaches a description call or registration processing must be checked separately in the references for the corresponding revision. If no connection is found, the investigation stops there.

## 2024-03-07: One sample overturned half of the original assessment

The counterexample retained after review did not identify a new source. It only shows that a description sample can also have no verifiable registration anomaly. This counterexample is enough to refute the simplified assumption that "any change in the description must be accompanied by registration", but not enough to explain why the descriptions differ or to show that all samples with no observed registration come from the same path.

As a result, triage was changed to record the description side first, then check whether comparable registration-side records exist. Previously, the first question was "Are we investigating registration?", which made it easy to put off examining the pre-call input; after the revision, the first question is "Is the pre-call state already different?". The registration issue was not removed; it can simply no longer use description differences as its own evidence.

```text
Description-side review
|
+-- Is there already a verifiable difference before the call?
|   +-- Yes: record the input and observation location, stop source attribution
|   `-- No or unknown
|       +-- Any additional changes after the call?
|       |   +-- Yes: record the change category and sequence
|       |   `-- No: retain the empty observation from this check
|       `-- Pre-call state missing: mark as incomplete
|
`-- Any direct observation on the registration side?
    +-- Yes: record separately, and cross-check when their relative timing can be compared
    `-- No: end the description branch
```

Change categories must not simply be labeled "description anomaly". Differences in element content, count, order, and observation location are four different kinds of observations. When a report says "there is one extra item", also confirm whether it means the count, the declaration index, or some kind of display ordering; without a sample, leave it unconfirmed. Lumping these terms together will cause later reviewers to misreport a difference in presentation as a change to the object itself.

The registration branch also has its own stopping points. Whether registration was actually being processed in that instance, the state in which the anomaly was seen after processing, and whether its timing relative to the description call can be compared are three things that cannot substitute for one another. When the registration observation precedes the description call, the description call cannot be used to explain registration; when the description call precedes the registration observation, this still does not justify saying that the description triggered registration. If the order cannot be confirmed, record only side-by-side observations.

## The abandoned combined table

There was also an interim attempt to put resource texture descriptions, diagnostic names, and concurrent registration into one table. The table had columns for "before the call", "after the call", "registration", and "diagnostic name", and looked more complete than the tree, but the most critical gaps remained: some records lacked the pre-call state, while others lacked a directly observed state after registration processing. Putting terms for both issues in the same row did not establish a relationship between the objects.

This table was later no longer maintained. The problem was not that the three objects could not appear together, but that it disguised "terms appearing together" as "a shared path has already been found." A row containing only a descriptor term and a registration term still cannot answer which call produced what result; a row containing only a diagnostic name and a descriptor term still cannot answer whether the declaration is referenced.

The alternative approach is deliberately narrower: the descriptor record covers the states before and after the call, the registration record covers the post-processing state, and the diagnostic-file lookup covers the name and declaration entry point. Only when all three actually have comparable references and ordering should their relationship be discussed in the same section. Otherwise, keep them separately. Another conclusion in the old table, "No additional changes are sufficient to rule out concurrency," was also marked as deprecated because it mistook not seeing something this time for it not happening.

This table still has archival value. It explains why old reports often made "diagnostic name checked" look like runtime evidence, and it also explains why later addenda required the input descriptor, call site, and observation location to be written separately. When reading old reports, blanks in the table are not default values; a blank means not yet observed.

## 2025-08-08: Field entry point after rewording

The most recent reorganization did not purge the historical sections; instead, it made object confirmation the entry point. First confirm whether the report concerns the result of a resource texture descriptor call or is merely repeating an old issue name. If it is only an old issue name, go to the diagnostic-name lookup; it cannot directly provide a descriptor-side conclusion.

After confirming the object, proceed on the descriptor side according to the before-and-after states: if a difference already existed before the call, record the input and observation location, and stop making the inference "the current call introduced the difference"; if a change is observed after the call, specify whether it concerns content, quantity, order, or observation location; if the pre-call state is missing, leave a gap. No branch changes meaning merely because concurrent registration appeared in the same run.

The registration side likewise starts by confirming the object. It counts as direct observation on the registration side only when that run actually processed a registration and the post-processing state in which the anomaly was observed can be identified. If there is only a topic, an old issue name, or a direction for follow-up, record it as pending verification. The descriptor side cannot use it as the cause, and the registration side cannot use a descriptor change as proof.

```text
Current parallel entry points
|
+-- Confirmed object for the descriptor call
|   +-- Before/after states complete: verify the descriptor result
|   `-- Incomplete state: leave only known fragments
|
+-- Confirmed state after registration processing
|   +-- Sequence comparable: record the sequence faithfully
|   `-- Sequence not comparable: record as parallel observations
|
`-- Any object not yet confirmed
    `-- Do not establish a relationship between the descriptor and registration
```

These stopping points are very specific in the field. If the call object is not confirmed, an issue name cannot be treated as the call result; if the pre-call state is missing, do not choose between the explanation that it already existed in the input and the explanation that it was produced after the call; if the registration side has no post-processing state, do not write the registration direction as an anomaly; if the ordering on the two sides cannot be compared, do not substitute textual order for event order. You can still retain samples and items to be filled in when stopping at a gap, but do not select the most similar-looking cause from old experience.

## 2025-08-11: Descriptor wording appended later

After retaining all the earlier old rules, review margin notes, diagnostic recheck failures, counterexamples, and merge-table issues, the current agreed interpretation of the confirmed call target is stated here: D2D1PixelShader.GetResourceTextureDescriptions<T>() returns ReadOnlyMemory<D2D1ResourceTextureDescription> with stable declared indices and dimensional ranks, using shared array-backed storage.

This interpretation constrains only the description branch. During verification, first confirm that the observation concerns the result of this call, then determine whether the reported difference is in the element content, count, declared indices, dimensional rank, or observation position. A report that only says "the array changed" is still insufficient, because it does not specify whether the change is in the object content, the index relationship, or the observation method enabled by shared-array backing. If these cannot be distinguished, keep the record on the description side.

Stable declared indices and dimensional ranks also do not mean that every "order" in historical reports has already been fully explained. Earlier reports often do not state whether the sample came from before or after the call, nor do they explain whether the comparison was of the description itself or some presentation order. Such reports can be clues for continued verification, but must not be recast as counterexamples to interface behavior.

This description interpretation does not define concurrent registration as a source or consequence of the description result. Registration is still recorded as a separate branch. Only when a single observation includes both the before-and-after states of the description call, the direct state after registration handling, and the ability to compare their order can the relationship between the two be discussed in the same passage; even when these conditions are met, record only the relationship actually observed, and do not expand parallel observations into causality.

The current recheck entry point is still `src/ComputeSharp.D2D1.SourceGenerators/Diagnostics/DiagnosticDescriptors.cs`. It can be used to verify the diagnostic name and declaration. To show that the name really leads to the description call or registration handling, you still need to find the connection in a reference for the corresponding revision; if you stop at the declaration only, record that stopping point. This path cannot substitute for evidence of the ordering of the description result.

## Margin issues not yet disentangled

"Order change" still has no consistent meaning. It may refer to a declared index, the presentation order of the description collection, or simply the comparison of two samples from different times. New records should first identify whether what is missing is a pre-call sample, a post-call sample, an observation position, or the comparison object itself; if that gap cannot be filled, remain in the description branch and do not switch to explaining registration.

Another adjacent issue is the relationship between the old issue name and the current call site. The diagnostic declaration can confirm whether the name exists, but cannot by itself explain the call path. In a follow-up, if only the name is found, it should still be written as "name checked"; if a reference is found but there is no runtime state, stop at the reference; only when the actual object, state, and sequence can all be matched should comparison between the two tracks continue.

Another documentation practice remains unresolved: some old samples combine "one more item," "order change," and "a different result was seen after the call" into one sentence. For now, do not choose an interpretation for these samples. They may remain alongside the original event, but separate the terms that can be confirmed from the objects that cannot be confirmed; otherwise, readers may mistakenly think that the old samples have already verified the declared indices or the registration relationship.

## Archival appendix: two shorthand phrases that will still turn up in searches

**"Description has one extra item; check registration first."**

This sentence gives no pre-call state, nor does it explain whether "one extra item" refers to a quantity, an index, or an observation position. For now, it can only be read as a descriptor observation and an unverified registration direction. We cannot infer from it that the current call changed the descriptor, nor that concurrency has already occurred.

**"The diagnostic name is in the same place, so the order should be consistent."**

This sentence treats the proximity of the diagnostic declarations as the runtime ordering, which is no longer applicable. Reviewing the file can verify the names, but cannot confirm the order, source, or registration handling of the descriptor results.

A more deliberate reminder was also once left in the margin: descriptor issues and registration issues can occur in the same round, but being in the same round does not establish a relationship. It does not fill in the missing sample in the historical record, but it can preserve the boundary between the input state, the call result, and the post-processing state.
