## descriptor-lifecycle-2026.09 public ABI clarification (repair-110-v1)
The fully qualified public interface is ComputeSharp.D2D1.Descriptors.ID2D1PixelShaderDescriptor<T>, where T : unmanaged, ComputeSharp.D2D1.ID2D1PixelShader. It has instance get-only properties (not static abstract members): ref readonly Guid EffectId; string? EffectDisplayName, EffectDescription, EffectCategory, EffectAuthor; int ConstantBufferSize, InputCount, ResourceTextureCount; ReadOnlyMemory<D2D1PixelShaderInputType> InputTypes; ReadOnlyMemory<D2D1InputDescription> InputDescriptions; ReadOnlyMemory<D2D1ResourceTextureDescription> ResourceTextureDescriptions; D2D1PixelOptions PixelOptions; D2D1BufferPrecision BufferPrecision; D2D1ChannelDepth ChannelDepth; D2D1ShaderProfile ShaderProfile; D2D1CompileOptions CompileOptions; string HlslSource; ReadOnlyMemory<byte> HlslBytecode. Its methods are T CreateFromConstantBuffer(ReadOnlySpan<byte> buffer) and void LoadConstantBuffer<TLoader>(in T shader, ref TLoader loader) where TLoader : struct, ComputeSharp.D2D1.Descriptors.ID2D1ConstantBufferLoader (a public interface with void LoadConstantBuffer(ReadOnlySpan<byte> data)). ReadOnlyMemory types are System.ReadOnlyMemory; unqualified D2D1 types resolve using ComputeSharp.D2D1 and ComputeSharp.D2D1.Interop. An empty HlslBytecode means no embedded precompiled shader. D2D1PixelShader forwarding preserves descriptor values. The public opt-in marker is ComputeSharp.D2D1.D2DGeneratedPixelShaderDescriptorAttribute. This is the target ABI to implement; missing baseline declarations are not evidence the requirement is out of scope.

The review still starts at `src/ComputeSharp.D2D1.SourceGenerators/Diagnostics/DiagnosticDescriptors.cs`. This file is a reference point from earlier investigations: issue names and call names lead readers to the area around the diagnostic declarations. It's useful for checking what the generator reports, but not for determining a particular caller's COM identity on its own.

The first draft put the two lines of investigation side by side because the symptoms seen at the time all looked like "no descriptor was produced." This time, the inputs were narrowed to two states of a single shader declaration: explicitly marked with opt-in, or without that marker. The comparison records only whether the descriptor enters the generation path; diagnostic text is no longer used to infer whether the native object still retains the same identity.

The counterexample here is useful too: looking for the cause in COM identity first makes it easy to mistake a caller-boundary issue for a descriptor issue. Conversely, having a descriptor does not mean that subsequent interop calls have no other restrictions. The two lines of investigation can share an entry point within the same investigation, but their notes should be kept separate.

This review confirmed the following on the generation side: D2DGeneratedPixelShaderDescriptorAttribute is a public opt-in marker; an opted shader receives a compilable generated descriptor implementing ID2D1PixelShaderDescriptor<T>.

So "marked" in these experiment notes does not mean the presence of just any attribute; it means that this public marker is applied to the shader. The check is not whether any helper type appears, but whether the generated descriptor compiles and implements the corresponding `ID2D1PixelShaderDescriptor<T>`. This is somewhat narrower than guessing from diagnostic names, and avoids recording the behavior of unmarked declarations as a failure.

COM identity remains a separate investigation. It has not been incorporated into the conclusion above, and the descriptor has not been treated as proof of native identity. If the investigation continues, an existing caller should be chosen, with the actual entry point and the result at the time recorded separately; don't merge the conclusions from the two sides just because the names are adjacent.

These notes have not been merged with the discussion of bytecode memory and AutoConstructor in DOC-16. That page covers compatibility history; this one records opt-in's direct observation of the generated descriptor.

# Embedded bytecode compatibility decision

When the old material on descriptor-lifecycle-2026.09 was being organized, embedded bytecode memory and AutoConstructor compatibility were discussed together. Both sit close to the descriptor lifecycle, but the leads available at the time weren't enough to describe them as a single implementation change. This page preserves the distinction made then; it continued to be cited as an older starting point, but wasn't maintained alongside the interface documentation.

There were two ways to document this at the time. One was to combine bytecode's memory representation and the automatic construction path into a single compatibility requirement, then check just one declaration later. That would be quick to record, but would conflate "whether the memory can be retained" and "whether the construction path is available" into one issue. The other was to record each issue separately, then provide a shared starting point for verification. # Matrix Intrinsic Storage Migration Notes

This record initially confined the matrix intrinsic storage issue to a very narrow entry point: the old investigation records pointed from the issue name and call name to `src/ComputeSharp.D2D1.UI/PixelShaderEffect{T}.ICanvasImageInterop.cs`, so the migration steps were written around this file. The initial goal was not to establish a complete descriptor graph, but to let old callers return to the original inspection point after the adjustment.

This entry point has never been moved. It did serve in the historical material as "where to start looking"; but it was later written more strongly than the material itself justified. The old draft treated the entry point, storage point, and migration landing point as the same thing, so readers following it could easily mistake the filename for implementation ownership. The original route and the recovery method used at the time are retained below, and this layer of confusion is also called out.

## Initial Migration Ticket

The task list at the time was short: for now, do not change effect names; if compatibility verification for matrix intrinsic required changing the caller, make both the new and old call names lead back to the same interop file; if that link broke, prioritize restoring the old call name. The reason was that the issue was first brought here by names and call relationships, not by an already organized storage inventory.

The judgments in the old ticket were as follows, with their original intent retained:

- `PixelShaderEffect{T}.ICanvasImageInterop.cs` was treated as the migration starting point for matrix intrinsic storage.
- When the caller could still reach this file from the old name, it was provisionally assumed that compatibility verification could continue.
- If the entry point could not be found, do not continue expanding the scope of changes; first return to the call name used before migration.
- Leave descriptor-related objects alone for now and wait for the result on the effect side.

Of these, the third item was once very useful. It prevented further changes to descriptions when the entry point had already been lost, turning one local backtrace into simultaneous changes to multiple objects. The second and fourth were overly optimistic: they treated "the entry point is still there" as "the storage relationship still holds," and put descriptor on the side that did not need synchronization.

The old route can be shown as follows:

```text
matrix intrinsic issue name
          |
          v
      Call-name lookup
          |
          v
src/ComputeSharp.D2D1.UI/PixelShaderEffect{T}.ICanvasImageInterop.cs
          |
          v
Old conclusion: this is the storage adjustment point
```

The final item is an old conclusion and should no longer be treated as a verified structural diagram. The file path is an investigation entry point; by itself, it provides no sufficient basis to confirm ownership of the matrix intrinsic storage implementation. The old version did not record the declarations inside the file, adjacent objects, and actual references item by item, so this diagram also cannot be used to infer how a specific memory manager, metadata, or binding slot has been handled.

## Actual Operations Between the Old Path and New Callers

During the migration batch, what needs to be preserved first is the trace-back path, not an abstract "compatibility state." For callers that still use the old name, first record their existing name, then open the file above and inspect the local declarations and nearby navigation available at the time. If the new caller has already been renamed, first use the old name to find the original landing point, then compare whether the new name can still return to the same place.

This comparison answers only one question: whether the names and call relationships still preserve the original entry point. It does not answer how matrix intrinsic values are stored, nor whether the effect output has already been rebuilt. The old draft merged these two questions, which is why it arrived at the claim that "as long as the entry point is there, storage compatibility carries no separate risk." This claim is retained as a historical judgment and is no longer a migration completion criterion.

When processing in the order of the old batch, the steps are:

1. Copy down the name used by the caller before migration; do not replace it with the issue title remembered from memory.
2. First use the name to return to `PixelShaderEffect{T}.ICanvasImageInterop.cs`, and confirm that the old entry point is still reachable.
3. If the new caller still lands here, record it only as "entry continuity"; do not record it as "storage confirmed."
4. If the new caller cannot land here, stop expanding changes on the descriptor side, restore the original call name, and then recheck.
5. When the file contains only local declarations or forwarding clues, record the result as pending investigation; do not infer who owns the implementation from the path location.

This sequence still describes the old migration method rather than a current unified integration rule. Its value lies in preserving the stopping point from that time: when the call name has lost the old entry point, first restore a state that can be checked; do not change the name, description, and effect-side objects at the same time. The old ticket does not provide enough evidence to support more aggressive recovery actions.

## Note Added After a Review

CSH-209 were later classified under release verification and taken up for processing, requiring the corresponding module maintainer to confirm the current behavior of matrix intrinsic and identify entry points that could still be checked. This changed how the document was used: the card can take people back to this page and the historical file path, but it does not provide an implementation description that can replace the old conclusion.

The review again found the starting point of the old investigation records: both the issue name and the call name pointed to this interop file. No direct evidence was found that would allow the document to assert that some object in the file holds matrix intrinsic storage. Therefore, the correction on this page goes only this far:

```text
Old wording: call name can reach file = storage point found
Corrected wording: call name can reach file = historical investigation entry point preserved
```

This correction deliberately does not supply a new final location to replace the old conclusion. The current material provides neither complete call relationships nor an explanation of which part among descriptor property contract, input type memory, and output construction is responsible for the intrinsic's actual storage. Filling in any one of these parts as the answer would turn a boundary that was originally unconfirmed into a definite fact.

## Retained Misleading Explanation

The passage below comes from the old migration guidance and continues to be retained to make it easier to understand why early callers closed out on the effect side:

> Since the matrix intrinsic issue appeared through an effect call, first complete the check at `PixelShaderEffect{T}.ICanvasImageInterop.cs`; descriptor does not need to be checked separately in the same batch.

This passage is not suitable as an operational premise now. It equates the call location where the issue appears with the location responsible for storage, and miswrites "do not change it in the same batch" as "does not need to be checked." It was not deleted because, when restoring old callers, we still encounter records made according to this wording; deleting it would instead make it impossible to see why the old batch stopped at this file.

Another old habit is likewise retained: as long as the call name is still present, assume that the matrix intrinsic migration has no independent risk. This habit was suitable at the time for preventing unrelated scope expansion, but it cannot substitute for checking actual references. At most, entry continuity shows that the old investigation trail has not been broken.

## Restore the Old Path

Returning to the old path is safer than continuing to guess when any of the following occurs: the new caller's name cannot be traced back to the original file; the file provides only interface or forwarding-layer clues; or the discussion has begun treating matrix intrinsic, descriptor, and effect output as a single change point.

Restoration consists of only two actions. First, roll back the new name introduced in this batch and restore the old name that callers could use before migration. Second, return from the old name to `src/ComputeSharp.D2D1.UI/PixelShaderEffect{T}.ICanvasImageInterop.cs` and use it as the starting point for the next verification. Do not add runtime rollback, memory-layout restoration, or bulk descriptor changes just because the entry point has been restored; these actions have not been established as one path in the existing records.

Being able to reach this file after restoration still does not mean that the issue is resolved. It only returns the investigation to a location that the old batch can recognize. If it remains impossible after restoration to identify the specific object responsible for storage, keep the unknown under matrix intrinsic storage; do not close it out with "the effect side has already been reviewed."

## Objects Still Missing

The latest note added to this page only narrowed the old judgment; it did not fill these gaps:

- The specific behavior corresponding to matrix intrinsic in the current version still needs confirmation from the module maintainer.
- The relationship between this interop file and the actual storage object still needs to be checked against the file contents and its references.
- Whether descriptor needs to be checked in the same batch as the caller can no longer be decided solely by the old effect entry point.
- The old material does not record whether the new and old names are equivalent when both can reach the entry point.

Therefore, `PixelShaderEffect{T}.ICanvasImageInterop.cs` continues to be the historical verification entry point for matrix intrinsic storage; "it is the storage adjustment point" is the old judgment retained on this page.

Doing so would miswrite an investigation clue as a decision.

Subsequent review should begin with the actual references to `D2D1PixelShaderEffect.cs`, confirm the relationship between this entry and effect registration XML, and only then determine whether the issue needs to be split out to a more specific object. # Effect Registration XML Decision Record

When this record was first created, effect registration XML was merely descriptor-lifecycle-2026. A string of names beside 09. It carried enough technical terms to be easily read as an implementation task whose location had already been identified: effect looked like an object, registration like an action, and XML like an artifact. The draft did not accept this reading. At that time, the only entry point that could be revisited repeatedly was `src/ComputeSharp.D2D1/Shaders/Interop/D2D1PixelShaderEffect.cs`, and what that entry point could establish was that it was worth starting the investigation there—not the complete relationship implied by the name.

This review did not rewrite the old record as a comprehensive registration design. The old judgment was retained because it explains why, during subsequent verification, tasks were not split directly by name; what was added was the set of paths compared at the time, the responsibility assigned to each path, and which statements could not be inferred from the existing materials.

## The Retained Starting Point

The old investigation record pointed both the issue name and the call name to `D2D1PixelShaderEffect.cs`. The file is located at `src/ComputeSharp.D2D1/Shaders/Interop` and belongs to the existing D2D1 interop module. The current index gives it a very narrow purpose: reading code and checking historical behavior. This purpose is more restrained, yet also more useful, than "the file where the registration implementation resides"; it tells the reviewer to first examine local declarations and adjacent objects, rather than treating the directory hierarchy as a conclusion about responsibility.

Here, "checking historical behavior" has a specific meaning. In the descriptor lifecycle materials, effect registration XML is a name that needs to be revisited, but no XML sample was delivered with this material, nor was a call record delivered that could directly link a declaration to XML. Thus, the name itself can only serve as a search term. It can help someone find the old record and code entry point, but it cannot replace confirmation of the reference relationship.

The draft initially included a very natural working assumption: since the filename contains `PixelShaderEffect`, effect registration XML was probably supposed to be handled here. This assumption was not absurd, but it was not evidence either. It mistakenly treated "being able to navigate to the same code area" as "the same code area owning responsibility for the output." During the review, no material was found sufficient to combine these two judgments, so the origin of this assumption was retained while its inferential force was withdrawn.

## The Fast Path Not Chosen at the Time

The easiest path to advance is to treat effect registration XML directly as an already-established artifact and create work items targeting XML, starting from the name. On the surface, this makes the descriptor lifecycle to-do clear: there is an object, an action, and a format. But the key premise it requires us to add is not in the record.

First, it is unclear whether XML refers to an existing visible output, an expected output, or a label used during checking. Each case leads to different follow-up work. If it is an existing output, the review should focus on where the output comes from; if it is an expected output, the focus should be on which boundary the absence occurs at; if it is merely a check name, it cannot be used to infer runtime behavior. The initial draft provides no basis for choosing among these three.

Second, it is unclear what specific action registration refers to in this historical record. It may be used to describe the registration of effect, or it may simply be a locator term that appears alongside XML. Without a call sequence, object state, or output fragment, writing it up as a fixed step would create a false sense of certainty.

Finally, descriptor lifecycle is not automatically equivalent to the lifecycle of a single file. This term frames the issue in the context of the object being described and its evolution, but does not provide complete boundaries for the object's creation, handoff, output, or release. If an implementation point is designated now as "part of the lifecycle," once it is later discovered that the reference relationship is not where expected, the old decision will instead mislead troubleshooting.

Therefore, the quick decomposition was not adopted. Not because XML or registration is unimportant, but because they still cannot carry the meaning required for a concrete implementation decision.

## Another path: first treat the name as a name

The retained approach is not to set the record aside, but to change the commitment made by the record. effect registration XML is retained as a naming clue in the requirements history; `D2D1PixelShaderEffect.cs` is retained as an entry point for tracing back through the code; the relationship between the two is marked as requiring confirmation from actual references.

This distinction may seem subtle, but it avoids two common confusions.

The first confusion occurs during search. Issue names, call names, and file names often use closely related vocabulary, especially words such as effect, descriptor, and interop, which recur at different layers. A search hit shows that these words are close to one another; it does not show that they already form an execution path. Treating a hit as proof of implementation will cause subsequent code reading to look only for snippets that support the original conclusion.

The second type of confusion occurs during handoff. Someone writes "XML is near this file", and the person taking over can easily read it as "XML is handled by this file". The former is navigation information, while the latter is a judgment about responsibility. The two statements differ by only a few words, but the follow-up actions are completely different: the former calls for opening the references and checking adjacent objects, while the latter leads directly to scheduling changes, tests, or regression archiving. The old record retains the first statement and does not elevate it to the second.

This is also the central trade-off in this decision record: it is better to require some extra reference tracing in the next review than to let a name match become a conclusion about implementation ownership too early.

## How to use the review entry point

The entry-point file should still be the first stop, but the reading order needs to be fixed to avoid guessing from the name all over again each time.

First confirm that the object currently being examined is indeed `src/ComputeSharp.D2D1/Shaders/Interop/D2D1PixelShaderEffect.cs`, then look at the file's local declarations and immediate neighbors. The goal here is not to quickly find the characters "XML", but to identify which symbols can connect local effect, descriptor, or interop relationships to actual references. If you find only the same word root without seeing a relationship, you should stop at "similar names".

Next, look back at the call name cited in the old investigation record. The call name was retained because it once led readers to this entry point; it is not a verified call edge. During review, record "the file can be found using this name" and "this name actually passes through the objects in the file" separately. The former can confirm that navigation still works, while only the latter may change the ownership judgment.

If the reference relationships point XML elsewhere, update the entry-point description rather than forcing it to remain in `D2D1PixelShaderEffect.cs` just to keep the old record tidy. This file's value lies in preserving the original verification path, not in having to be the final destination. Conversely, if the relationships do converge here, also specify which part of the local relationship converges here; do not add a blanket statement of implementation ownership based only on "it ended up here after all".

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> NameClue
    NameClue --> SourceRecheck
    SourceRecheck --> ConfirmedLocalRelationships
    SourceRecheck --> PendingRelationships
    ConfirmedLocalRelationships --> RecordRetained
    PendingRelationships --> RecordRetained
```

The diagram's "PendingRelationships" is not a failure state. It indicates that the current material is sufficient to preserve the name and the entry point, but not sufficient to link the two to a specific responsibility. The old record deliberately stops at this state; removing the pending state would only mislead later readers into thinking that a full attribution had already been completed.

## Constraints on descriptor lifecycle

This decision does not define a new phase model for descriptor lifecycle. The material does not provide a complete sequence of creation, passing, destruction, or recreation, so there is no reason to invent a seemingly complete lifecycle diagram here. The only thing that can be confirmed here is this: effect registration XML is discussed as part of this history, so it should be retained as part of the relevant historical account; it does not automatically establish where XML falls in the lifecycle.

This distinction affects how regression documentation is written. "effect registration XML appeared" cannot be treated directly as a success condition, nor can "XML was not seen" be treated directly as a failure condition. When no visible output, inspection interface, or before-and-after states are provided, such statements merely disguise the issue's name as a verification result. The regression intent that can currently be retained is narrower: whenever entry-point relationships are reconfirmed, do not lose the historical fact that effect, registration, XML, and descriptor lifecycle were once raised as related topics.

In other words, the regression checkpoint for now is the relationship itself, not the text of some undelivered sample. Only if reliably identifiable output or call relationships become available later can this be upgraded to a more specific check. When upgrading it, state what type of evidence has been added: references, output, or object state. Do not retroactively present evidence obtained later as a fact already established in the initial draft.

## Responsibility Boundaries

File paths, issue names, and historical labels each serve different roles.

| Object | Role in this record | What cannot be concluded from it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| effect registration XML | A requirements clue left in descriptor-lifecycle-2026.09 | Whether it is an existing output, or who generates it |
| `D2D1PixelShaderEffect.cs` | The first entry point for code reading and historical cross-checking | Whether it alone is responsible for implementing XML or registration |
| Call names in earlier investigation records | Navigation criteria that lead from historical issues to the entry point | A verified call sequence or runtime path |
| descriptor lifecycle | The context for preserving the issue's history | A complete object phase model |

This table is not shifting the unknowns onto others. It lists the boundaries that this decision itself must not cross. The second row in particular: a source-code entry point is enough to begin an inspection, but not enough to assign responsibility for changes to a specific implementation point. These boundaries can be confirmed or refuted through subsequent code reading; until then, the record should not substitute file names for conclusions.

DOC-22 discusses bounded manager bindings. It and this record are part of the same round of D2D contract materials, but no material shows that manager bindings can explain effect registration XML, nor does any material show that XML can explain the boundaries of bindings. The two records therefore retain only cross-navigation links and are not merged into a single decision. Forcing similar terminology into a single design chain would obscure the aspects of each object that still need confirmation.

## Correction after a review

The wording in the initial draft could easily lead readers to interpret "reproduce starting from the pre-call state" as an already defined reproduction procedure. A later review of the retained material showed that this sentence only says to start observing from the pre-call state to see whether effect registration XML shows any additional visible changes; it provides no invocation steps, state snapshots, or expected output.

The old sentence should therefore no longer be treated as executable test instructions. It is still valuable because it identifies where the differences of interest lay at the time: the focus is not on searching for a piece of XML in isolation, but on comparing the states before and after a particular call to see whether any changes are left behind. But the objects, methods, and criteria needed for that "comparison" have not yet been captured in this record. Expanding it into commands, examples, or fixed assertions would go beyond the available material.

This correction also changes the meaning of "confirmation complete." Previously, it was easy to interpret completion as discovering a connection to XML somewhere. Now, the following two things are simply kept distinct: confirming that the navigation entry point is still usable, and confirming that the actual relationship has been established. The former is work that can be completed by maintaining this record; the latter requires support from reference relationships or observable results. The two are not interchangeable.

## Decisions made

The current decision consists of four complementary constraints.

1. Continue to retain effect registration XML in the requirements history for descriptor-lifecycle-2026.09, without removing this name from historical materials.
2. Retain `src/ComputeSharp.D2D1/Shaders/Interop/D2D1PixelShaderEffect.cs` as the first entry point for code investigation, because earlier investigation records did in fact lead here through the issue name and the call name.
3. Until actual reference relationships are established, do not record this file as the implementation location for effect registration XML, or record registration as a confirmed single step.
4. Any subsequent material intended to change this decision must add content that distinguishes navigation relationships from actual relationships; a closer name match alone is not enough to overturn the current boundary.

The third point here is especially important. It does not deny that the file may be related to the issue, but limits what the current record can claim. A mature decision can include deferring a conclusion: what is being deferred is not whether investigation is worthwhile, but a judgment about responsibility that cannot yet be pinned down from the available materials.

## Relationship to Quality and Regression

This page is categorized under Quality and Regression in the knowledge base, but that does not mean it already comes with a complete test plan. This classification reflects the fact that it preserves a relationship that needs to be revisited over the long term: a historical requirement name, a code entry point, and a decision that did not mistake a name for a conclusion. For subsequent regression work, the first mistake to avoid is losing sight of this decision and once again treating similarity in wording as proof of behavior.

If concrete effect registration XML samples become available later, document their sources, the conditions under which they occur, and where they were observed in a new record, then decide whether to link them to this entry point. If only new name matches emerge later, update only the navigation notes, not the behavioral assessment. If the old call name is later found to no longer lead to this file, preserve the fact that the old navigation route once existed, and record the new entry point separately; do not silently overwrite the old path and make the historical investigation appear never to have taken a detour.

For descriptor lifecycle, it is likewise inappropriate to turn an as-yet unconfirmed XML name into the sole quality signal. It can serve as an anchor for searches and reviews, but the current materials do not support extending it to cover other descriptor objects, other outputs, or other interop relationships. Expanding it into a global rule would distort a genuine local judgment.

## Card Entry Point

CSH-211 documents the verification of the existing check for effect registration XML: reproduce it starting from the pre-call state and observe whether any additional visible changes remain after completion. The card is a suitable place to record whether this check was completed; this decision record preserves why implementation ownership cannot be determined solely from the check name or entry-point file.

If follow-up actions on the card produce new visible changes, the card can serve as supplementary material for this page, but it does not automatically become a replacement for this decision. Conversely, if the card only proves that the check was run, the boundary defined here must still be maintained: running a check once does not mean that the full relationship between XML and `D2D1PixelShaderEffect.cs` has been explained.

## Questions that remain pending until the actual relationships emerge

The following questions were not resolved by this review, and keeping them open is more accurate than writing a seemingly complete conclusion.

- What exactly does effect registration XML refer to in this history: an artifact, an expectation, or a check label?
- Can the call name mentioned in the old troubleshooting records be confirmed from actual references involving `D2D1PixelShaderEffect.cs`?
- If there are visible changes, do they pertain to descriptor information, effect registration, or another adjacent object?
- If the entry point eventually moves elsewhere, should the old file be retained for historical navigation, or should the new relationships replace it as the primary entry point?

These questions do not prevent the current decision from taking effect. The decision has already made clear how to preserve the materials while answers are still unavailable: preserve the names, preserve the entry points, preserve the origins of the old assumptions, and refuse to let them stand in for the actual relationships.

# Nested Constant Buffer Troubleshooting Tree

This record was originally intended only to prevent one very common misstep: a report mentions nested constant-buffer packing, so troubleshooting starts directly with the innermost members, and eventually no one can even establish whether the input shape, description materials, and call entry point belong to the same case. The tree from the first draft is therefore still kept here. It is suitable for stopping reports with incomplete materials at the entry point, not for judging layout by the appearance of the outer fields.

This review has not added a sample to this page that can stand in for all inputs. The old entry point is still available for inspection, but the path itself provides only local declarations and navigation to adjacent locations. The branches below therefore retain many stopping points: first separate the materials available, then decide whether to continue, rather than using the single word "packing" to lump together the descriptor, description memory, and call results.

## Collect materials before attributing a cause

For each report, first record three things: the member structure of the input type; the input description memory obtained from the same call; where the caller enters. These three items do not require a fixed format, nor do they require a complete incident record to be written in one pass. If only the type is available, just record the type; if only the symptoms are available, keep the symptoms together with the entry point and wait for the missing materials.

Document the outer object and nested object separately. For the outer object, state only which members it contains, and for the nested object, state the order of its own members. Once the fields from both levels are flattened into a single list, the names may appear to match, but the boundaries have already been lost. When someone later sees "the field counts are the same", they cannot tell whether the comparison was at the same level, or whether two levels just happened to have been combined into the same count.

Matrices should not be recorded as "a few numeric fields" either. When matrix intrinsic storage appears in the input, note whether it is at the outer or nested level; without this location, later comparisons can easily conflate the matrix with adjacent ordinary members. This does not identify the matrix as a cause, but merely prevents its identity from being lost in the materials.

If the report contains only numeric descriptor metadata, do not proceed to discuss nested boundaries yet. metadata can point to the next object to inspect, but it cannot replace the input members, nor can it replace input description memory. The old draft treated metadata together with the outer fields as sufficient material; this has now been changed to "can be recorded, but cannot establish the nature of the issue".

```text
Received a nested constant-buffer packing report
|
+-- Is the input type complete?
|   |
|   +-- No
|   |   |
|   |   +-- Record the known entry point or symptoms.
|   |   +-- Stop: add the outer members, nested members, and matrix location.
|   |
|   +-- Yes
|       |
|       +-- Only ordinary numeric members?
|       |   |
|       |   +-- Yes: check numeric descriptor metadata first;
|       |   |         do not record the nested boundary as reproduced.
|       |   |
|       |   +-- No: list the nested level separately.
|       |
|       +-- Is there matrix intrinsic storage?
|           |
|           +-- Yes: note its level, then enter the description branch.
|           +-- No: continue.
|
+-- Is input description memory from the same call available?
|   |
|   +-- No
|   |   |
|   |   +-- Do not compare field order.
|   |   +-- Do not use effect registration XML as a substitute input description.
|   |   +-- Stop: add description materials.
|   |
|   +-- Yes
|       |
|       +-- Does the description still retain the outer and nested levels?
|           |
|           +-- No: record the description-side difference, preserving both sides as they are.
|           +-- Yes: inspect member order level by level, without guessing boundaries from names.
|
+-- Is the call entry point known?
    |
    +-- No: do not attribute this to descriptor or interop, stop.
    |
    +-- Yes
        |
        +-- Does the current call pass through the old code entry point?
        |   |
        |   +-- No: record the actual entry point, do not force the investigation down the old path.
        |   +-- Yes: continue examining the description and results in that call.
        |
        +-- Does the result come from another caller?
            |
            +-- Yes: open a separate record, do not merge it with the current input.
            +-- No: enter the results branch.
```

"Stop" in the tree does not mean closing the issue. It only fixes the next step on the missing materials. Continuing to discuss field order without an input type only creates speculation that cannot be checked later; switching to effect registration XML when description memory is missing can only confirm that effect-related materials exist, not replace the input description. The first draft used XML as a stand-in when the description was missing, and that old approach is no longer used.

## The old approach to description comparison and its corrections

The first draft's "outer first, then inner" approach is retained because outer-level information can indeed help confirm whether two sets of materials concern the same kind of input. However, it is only a reading order. Matching outer appearances do not mean that the inner members have made it into the same description, nor do they mean that constant buffer reconstruction has handled the input correctly.

After obtaining input description memory, first check whether the description has preserved the hierarchical relationships. If the description retains only outer-level information, record "no nested hierarchy is visible on the description side", rather than directly rewriting this as "the nested members were discarded". The latter statement requires results from the same call and a more specific comparison; this page has not preserved a general-purpose sample of that kind.

When the description and type can be matched level by level, then check whether the descriptor property contract applies to the current object. The purpose here is very narrow: confirm that the property description and the current input have not been conflated in the record. The property contract and constant-buffer reconstruction are adjacent in the reading order, but they are not the same check. The old record put both in the same branch, making it impossible, when differences later appeared, to tell whether properties or buffer materials had actually been compared.

If the accounts of the type, description, and metadata come from different calls, do not invent a connection between them. Keeping them separate will make later tracing slower, but is more reliable than combining them into a "reproduced nesting issue". Symptoms involving the same type through different entry points should not automatically be treated as the same case either.

## Looking back from the old entry point

The old troubleshooting record traced the issue name and call name to `src/ComputeSharp.D2D1.UI/PixelShaderEffect{T}.ICanvasImageInterop.cs`. This is still where we start reading, because it is the code entry point left on this page. After opening it, first ask one very small question: whether the call at hand actually passes through this adjacent point.

If it does not pass through there, record the actual entry point and stop tracing the old path. Do not attribute the implementation to that file simply because its name resembles the issue. If it does pass through there, retain only three things from the current call: where the input type enters; whether input description memory can be obtained before and after the call; which caller produced the observed result. Copying out the entire effect registration, resource binding, and effect XML path is actually unhelpful for this kind of boundary.

The old notes once said "finding the file means the issue has been located". That was a shorthand left at the time to keep troubleshooting moving, and it is no longer treated as a status. The existence of the file only means that the old entry point can still be read; whether the call actually passes through it must still be stated separately in the current record.

interop is not treated as the default cause here either. When the entry point is unknown, descriptor, interop, and the caller all remain candidate areas. First using the actual entry point to narrow those areas, then recording differences in the description materials or results, will save some detours compared with working backward from module names to causes.

## Separate results by symptom

Once the materials are complete, first record what is observed, then where to look next. When the type and description hierarchies cannot be matched, preserve both sides as they are and mark this as a description-side difference; do not use outer field counts in place of nested boundaries. If the type and description can still be matched but the call results differ, preserve the result actually seen by the caller, and continue tracing back through the connections around constant-buffer reconstruction.

Neither branch can be recorded directly as the final cause. A description-side difference does not automatically mean that descriptor output is wrong; a matching description with different results does not automatically mean that buffer reconstruction is faulty either. The old record's value is only to bring the next step back to an object that can be inspected when different symptoms appear, rather than letting "packing" become a catch-all label for every difference.

If the type, description, and results currently show no differences, do not mark the original report as normal either. First check whether the entry point in the report is the same as the current entry point. If the report comes from another caller and the input materials do not match one to one, split it into another record and do not assign a common cause.

Temporarily flattening nested objects should not be used as a recovery action. Flattening directly changes the input shape; even if the symptoms disappear, this only shows that the object being compared has changed, and cannot explain the original nested boundary. Likewise, if removing the matrix changes anything, first record "the input shape has changed", rather than immediately identifying matrix intrinsic storage as the cause.

## Old branches still retained

The following practices are no longer valid decision criteria in this tree, but are retained here to prevent them from later being mistaken for completed verification:

- Compare only the outer fields, then infer that the nested members are aligned.
- When input description memory is missing, look only at effect registration XML.
- After finding the old code path, directly mark the issue as located.
- Substitute the results from the flattened object for the results from the original nested input.

These actions are not entirely without value. Outer fields can help filter materials; XML can help confirm effect-related records; flattened input can serve as a separate comparison object. The problem is that none of them can independently answer what happened to the original nested input. Later records should list them as comparisons already performed, not as conclusions about recovery.

generated marshalling attributes are not included in this tree. They belong to a separate line of compatibility checks; if the change in the current materials is attribute generation rather than nested member structure, go to DOC-24 and leave a local record. Keeping them separate does not assert that the two are unrelated, only that this old investigation did not verify the relationship.

## Minimum requirements for a field record

When continuing to use this page, a record can be very short, but it must at least let the next reader distinguish where the materials came from:

- The outer object, nested object, and the level containing the matrix.
- The input description memory from the same call, or an explicit statement that it is missing.
- The call entry point; if tracing back from the old entry point, state whether passage through it has been confirmed.
- Whether the observation is a hierarchy mismatch, different call results, or an issue that has not yet been reproduced.
- Comparisons already performed: examining only the outer level, examining only XML, flattening the input, or other actions that change the input shape.

Do not add fixed offsets, byte counts, exception text, or commands; this page did not retain those details. Prioritize finding a caller that still uses this input shape, and check the actual version, entry point, and current results. If even one of those three items is still missing, stop troubleshooting at the missing item, rather than reshaping the old tree into a seemingly complete layout rule.

# HLSL Writer Decision Record

What this record originally captured was not an implementation plan, but a point of reference that could easily be misread. As descriptor-lifecycle-2026.09 began to be consolidated, the name pooled HLSL writer had already appeared among the investigation leads; following the issue name and call names led to `src/ComputeSharp.SourceGeneration.Hlsl/SyntaxRewriters/ShaderSourceRewriter.cs`. The code index also listed this file as an existing module, suitable for reading the code and checking historical behavior.

At the time, the easiest approach would have been to assume that the path identified where the writer's lifecycle was managed, then plan all subsequent changes on the rewriter side. The initial draft did not do that. Being able to find the file through older records only showed that it was on the investigation path used at the time; it did not, on its own, show that the object was acquired, reused, or returned there, or that its configuration was held there. This distinction remained useful later, so the initial draft was not trimmed down to a vague "to be confirmed".

There were actually two options on the table at the time.

- Treat `ShaderSourceRewriter.cs` as the implementation location for the pooled HLSL writer, and continue investigating changes on that basis.
- Keep it as a historical entry point on the source output side, and include it in the implementation assessment only once the reference relationships were sufficient to show that the lifecycle passed through that point.

The second option was adopted. It did not assert that the writer definitely could not be near that file; it only rejected using filenames and old investigation leads in place of reference relationships. For descriptor-lifecycle, this was especially important: visible adjacency on the source output side and the location of an object's lifecycle are not the same question. The former is enough to determine where to look first, while the latter requires more narrowly scoped code relationships.

## The Narrow Scope Retained from the Initial Draft

The initial draft's phrase "trace the generation path back from the rewriter" remains valid, but its role is navigation. Readers can start from this file to examine neighboring objects related to generation, or use it to check why the older records led to the source generation side. It does not mean that pooling of the pooled writer has been proven to take place within this file, nor does it mean that all descriptor configuration passes through this entry point.

Another earlier assessment was "establish the actual references first". This was not a request to first draw a complete call graph of the entire generator, nor to cram every possible configuration item into the same record. What needs to be established here is the segment of the relationship that connects the pooled writer to a specific lifecycle location. If that relationship does indeed lead back to the rewriter, the entry point in the initial draft will become part of the implementation assessment; if it leads elsewhere, the old entry point still retains its historical value.

The initial draft also deliberately made no decision to replace any existing generation path. That was not because pooling was unimportant, but because there was not enough material at the time to establish the existing writer's ownership, concurrency boundaries, or caching relationships. Turning "it should be pooled" directly into "it should be replaced within the rewriter" would skip over two still-unconfirmed questions at once. This conservative approach was the decision at the time, not a description of the later implementation state.

## Records from the Follow-up Review

CSH-216 later put this lead back in the review queue. The card called for checking the configuration closure involved in the "pooled HLSL writer" change, and following up on each missing item in the corresponding repository file. Here, configuration closure means the set of configuration items that need to be checked together for this change; the card did not provide an already-completed list of items.

The card had one dependency_checked action. This action addressed the shortcoming of the initial draft, which had stopped entirely at locating by name: at least one round of dependency checking had been recorded. But it did not establish `ShaderSourceRewriter.cs` as the definite location of the writer's lifecycle. Dependency checking answers which configuration relationships involved in the change need further follow-up in files; it does not automatically answer where the writer is acquired or returned. These two things may be adjacent, or they may be separate.

The review was then marked Blocked, with the reason given that an account with standard permissions had not yet been activated. This status explains why the check did not proceed further, but provides no new conclusions about the runtime behavior of source output, descriptor, or pooling. The gaps in the initial draft were therefore not filled, and there was simply a clearer work status: a dependency check had been performed, and further verification was blocked by access conditions.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> HistoricalInvestigationEntryPoint
    HistoricalInvestigationEntryPoint --> DependenciesChecked
    DependenciesChecked --> AccessBlocked
    AccessBlocked --> ReferencesPending
```

This sequence of states is not an implementation flowchart. It preserves only the order in which this decision record's understanding developed: first a file entry point reached by name, then a dependency check, then a stop caused by account conditions, and finally a return to the original issue of reference relationships still needing to be established. Reading "DependenciesChecked" in the diagram as "pool verified" would go beyond the card's action itself.

## Interpretations Not Adopted

The first interpretation not adopted was that because HLSL source output passes through the rewriter, the pooled writer's lifecycle must also pass through the rewriter. This reasoning lacks an intermediate relationship. The source output is the context for this historical lead, not substitute evidence of object ownership.

The second interpretation not adopted was to close all issues on the descriptor-lifecycle side on the basis of dependency_checked. The dependency check itself is worth retaining, but the card called for following up on missing items in the corresponding repository files; it did not say that every item had been covered, nor did it assign every configuration item to the same path. A single action therefore cannot be expanded into a complete configuration conclusion.

The third interpretation not adopted was to classify the fact that an account with standard permissions had not yet been activated as a technical risk for the writer. It was an access limitation on the review. Keeping this distinction prevents later readers from misrecording an inability to continue inspecting as an implementation failure, or mistakenly assuming that the rewriter had been ruled out because of a permissions issue.

One sentence in the initial draft could sound too strong: "The actual references need to be established first, before deciding whether the configuration items in descriptor-lifecycle are covered by this entry point." This sentence remains, but is now understood more narrowly. It describes the verification needed to determine whether this entry point can cover a particular configuration item, rather than requiring all descriptor configuration to pass through the HLSL rewriter. The older wording has not been completely replaced because it accurately records why changes were not made directly on the basis of the path at the time.

## The Decision That Remains in Effect

This record continues to treat `src/ComputeSharp.SourceGeneration.Hlsl/SyntaxRewriters/ShaderSourceRewriter.cs` as the historical entry point for investigating the pooled HLSL writer, not as the definite implementation location of the writer's lifecycle. Compared with the initial draft, this decision has two additional pieces of context from CSH-216: the dependency check and the access blockage, but neither has changed the conclusion.

When further verification becomes possible, first check the configuration closure involved in the change in accordance with the requirements of CSH-216, and follow up on any missing items found in the corresponding repository files; then determine whether the actual relationship between the rewriter and the pooled writer is sufficient to update this record. If the reference relationships show that the writer is acquired or returned in this file, an implementation assessment can be appended after this decision. If the relationships lead elsewhere, there is no need to retroactively delete the old entry point either: it still explains why this lead originally began on the source generation side.

This page preserves the boundaries of a decision at an earlier point in time. It should not be treated as a description of the current implementation of the pooled HLSL writer; but when reviewing the history of descriptor-lifecycle, it still explains why the modification location was not specified solely on the basis of a file path.

# Postmortem: Unmerged Performance Lab Records

This anomaly did not present as a clear failed run. The entry point still opened, but the boundary sample differed from the old record. Investigation found that the current revision entries for two revisions had been placed under the same entry point; readers could not tell which record the values on the page belonged to. These are the incident notes from that time, without filling gaps in later evidence with conclusions.

## When the difference was noticed

The first clue was simply that the boundary sample did not match the old record. This was initially treated as a missing-record issue: the same entry point contained two sections of content, but there were no markers to distinguish them. Since both sections were treated as current results, repeatedly reading the entry point did not reveal whether this was a record-level or run-level issue.

The scope of affected usage was not confirmed at the time. What was confirmed was that the entry point itself displayed two revisions side by side, and that the second section was not an empty placeholder. It was not possible to confirm which section was written first or which one later overwrote the display slot. Nor were enough timestamps retained to put the two results in a reliable order.

## Incident handling

Further retries provided no new way to distinguish the two. The version of `docs/adj-samples/incidents/samples-performance-lab-two-version-records-not-merged.md` from that time was therefore preserved, and subsequent read results were no longer appended to the same record. This only froze the incident state; it did not prove that the two executions had been saved separately.

Later checks showed that the memory manager could recover, so the concern that "the entire run had become unrecoverable" no longer held. This finding did not explain why the bytecode had changed; that question remained open alongside the original record. In other words, recovery meant the incident state could continue to be read, not that there was evidence that the two versions of the record had been merged.

## Impact

The direct impact of mixing the records under one entry point was a loss of comparison context. Against the old record, the boundary sample difference looked like a change in results; against the other section in the entry point, an old value could instead be mistaken for the current one. Both readings occurred during the incident, so this page cannot support a single conclusion about execution.

At the time, speculation about adjacent services was not recorded as a cause, and no run order was fabricated. Only if the current revision left by the second read or run can be recovered later will there be a basis for matching the two sections back up; if only the final state remains, this gap stays open.

## Archive location

The original record is still in the incident file mentioned above. It is useful as a starting point for review, especially when someone remembers only "two revisions on the same page" but has forgotten the boundary sample difference. However, its early statements about run state are from that time and should not replace a separate investigation into the bytecode change.

versions.body:
# Performance Lab Failed-Run On-Call Procedure

Use this procedure when a run of samples-performance-lab shows an anomaly, or when the on-call engineer can confirm only part of the pre-failure state. Start at `docs/adj-samples/runbooks/samples-performance-lab-failed-run-on-call-page.md`; do not start a separate record from a similar page in the directory.

## Preserve the state first

1. Find the `descriptor` for this run. If there is no descriptor at the entry point, stop here and record the last object that can still be confirmed; do not fill in the run scope with defaults.
2. Check the `metadata` next to the descriptor. The presence of metadata only means that this part of the state is visible. Do not treat it as successful execution, and do not clean up or overwrite the original contents first.
3. Check `source output`. This on-call record treats source output not appearing as the first failure point. If there is still no source output at this step, stop recovery actions and do not keep guessing about downstream artifacts.

If the observed state already includes a run id, trace, or version information, preserve those original values as well. If those values are absent, write only "not seen"; do not substitute the current revision for the pre-failure state. In particular, if collection or execution cannot be confirmed to have actually occurred, `current revision` remains unknown.

## Branch checks

- **No descriptor**: There is insufficient evidence at the entry point; this is not a signal that the run can be retried. Preserve the last confirmable pre-failure state, return to the current entry point, and wait for a record that identifies a specific descriptor.
- **Descriptor present, no metadata**: Do not clean up the state or adjust parameters first. Record that the descriptor was seen and metadata was not seen, then stop at this step.
- **Metadata present, no source output**: Leave metadata unchanged and mark missing source output as the first failure. Do not interpret missing output as empty output; do not continue processing the downstream `bytecode`, `cache`, or `extent`.
- **Source output present, but the result is still abnormal**: Save source output first, then separately record any visible `bytecode`, `cache`, `extent`, and `concurrency`. These names identify only objects in the observed state; they do not by themselves establish which layer failed. If any item comes from an old record, label it as an old value and do not overwrite this run's value.

Do not change both `binding slot` and `concurrency` during the same check. If either has already been changed, stop comparing and preserve the visible records from before and after the change; do not treat the result after both changes as a single-variable observation. Do not clear cache before saving source output either, or it will be impossible to tell whether the failure occurred before output generation or after the cache change.

## Stop and roll back

After the first failure, stopping means: do not delete descriptor or metadata; do not clear cache; do not release or reassign the binding slot without authorization; do not record an unknown current revision as the executed version. Roll back only local state explicitly changed during this on-call work. Recovery actions have not yet been tried in the shared environment, so do not record a local reproduction, reopening the entry point, or rereading metadata as successful recovery.

If new source output has already been generated, save the original and new outputs side by side before deciding whether to close out this on-call work. If there is no original output, record only "cannot compare"; do not infer it from bytecode or extent. Create a separate record for any rerun that requires changing multiple conditions; do not merge its results into this failed run on this page.

## Entry point for the next shift

Start the handoff from the same file entry point: `docs/adj-samples/runbooks/samples-performance-lab-failed-run-on-call-page.md`. The handoff only needs four items reflecting the actual state: whether descriptor was found, whether metadata was preserved, whether source output appeared, and whether current revision is still unknown. If binding slot, cache, or concurrency has already been touched, also state whether the change occurred before or after the first failure.

Do not write only "handled." At a minimum, leave the first step where work stopped and the objects that remain unconfirmed. The next shift should check the original state before deciding whether to attempt recovery; keep this limitation on the page until recovery actions in the shared environment have actual results.

# Postmortem: Unmerged Caller Integration Test Records

The entry point for caller integration testing once held "current revision" records for two revisions at the same time. The first discrepancy noticed was that opt-in did not match the old record. At the time, it looked like an error in a single record. Only after reviewing the entry point did we confirm that materials from two different points in time had not been kept separate, making it impossible to tell from the entry point which version was the guidance usable for current integration.

## Symptoms and Impact

The issue was at the entry point for caller integration test materials for adj-computesharp, not a confirmed runtime failure. The entry point retained both versions without clearly placing the older one in a historical location or displaying the later record separately as the current version. Anyone opening that location would first encounter two sets of guidance side by side, then have to decide which one to use to interpret opt-in.

The confirmed impact is limited to the records and integration decisions:

- The content of opt-in differed from the old record;
- The same entry point did not identify a single definitive version;
- With both records side by side, the older version would still be read as current material.

The extent of adoption has not been established. The materials do not state which callers had integrated against either revision, or whether the discrepancy extended beyond the records to affect actual calls. We therefore cannot classify all callers as affected or directly attribute the interop change to the mixed versions at the entry point.

## Sequence of Events

| Stage | What was observed at the time | Action taken at the time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Initial discovery | opt-in differed from the old record. | Investigated it as a discrepancy in a single record; the version relationship at the entry point had not yet been identified. |
| Review of the entry point | "Current revision" records for two revisions were at the same entry point. | Withdrew the assessment that only one piece of guidance was inconsistent, and preserved the evidence as a case of mixed versions. |
| Further retries stopped | New attempts would continue to change the combination of materials at the entry point. | Stopped combining the two records into one unified explanation. |
| Version preservation | The content as found remains in the incident file. | Preserved the version from that time; adj-computesharp continues to maintain the body and attachments. |
| Recovery observation | packing could recover. | Recorded only the packing recovery, not recovery of integration testing as a whole. |
| Follow-up review | The review only verified the current entry point. | Branches that could not be reproduced remained open for investigation. |

Specific timestamps are missing for each step. The available sequence only establishes that the opt-in discrepancy was found first, and the two revisions were then seen side by side at the entry point. Retries were stopped after the evidence had been preserved, and the packing recovery was a later observation. These do not form a complete operational timeline, and the last observed recovery state cannot override the initial discrepancy in the records.

The initial assessment was retained because it explains why the investigation continued to focus on opt-in: at that point, it was not yet apparent that the entry point held two versions at once. That assessment no longer applied after the review. Simply comparing the old and new records would not resolve the issue; the entry point did not convey their chronological order or intended uses. Rewriting the two sets of content into a single compromise explanation would lose the version boundary that actually existed when the issue was discovered.

## Evidence Preservation and Recovery Assessment

`docs/adj-computesharp/incidents/ComputeSharp-client-integration-two-version-records-not-merged.md` retains the version from that time. Keeping the old record does not mean it remains usable for current integration; it only preserves the fact that two versions once appeared side by side at the entry point. Further retries were stopped to prevent new results from overwriting the combination of materials that had been found, which would make it impossible to review the opt-in discrepancy.

The observation that packing could recover needs to be considered on its own. It shows that packing was recoverable in a later state, but does not show that the two revisions were no longer mixed at the entry point or explain why interop changed. If the packing result had previously been used as evidence that integration testing had recovered, that would conflate the issue in the records, the state of packing, and the unexplained interop change.

DOC-32 contains a migration index for the current and old entry points. This page does not add migration steps; it only records the issue in which the materials referenced by the index had not been kept separate at the entry point. To determine where the entry points lead, refer back to DOC-32, but do not infer from this that the two revisions have already been merged.

## Still Unconfirmed

Why interop changed is still unknown. It may simply be a discrepancy that only became visible once the two revisions were placed side by side, or it may be unrelated to packing; there is no material available to settle which explanation is correct. The second reviewer followed the original entry point and verified the current content, but did not reproduce the other branches, so those branches were not included in the assessment of the cause.

The extent of adoption is also unclear. The available records are insufficient to distinguish which callers read the older version, which encountered only the later version, or which never went through that entry point at all. Until these questions are resolved, the two versions of the materials can only be retained as historical evidence and investigative leads, not merged into a single current conclusion.

# Dependency Boundary Entry Point Migration Procedure

The index still starts at `docs/adj-license/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. It covers dependency sources, adoption scopes, and exit responsibilities associated with license; each item has its own adoption scope and exit conditions. Old entry points, replacement locations, and callers still using them are kept in the same index to make it easier to see whether a migration batch is actually complete.

The previous version treated `effect XML` as an exit point that should be separate, while leaving `bytecode` on the old entry point side. That judgment was only a working assumption at the time: different failure exits in the two segments do not mean that each path already has a complete consumer list. The list of active callers for `cache` is also still incomplete.

Before migrating, first copy the old entry points and callers into the index one by one. Each entry should retain at least: the entry point name visible to the consumer, the object it uses, the replacement location, and the old location to restore on rollback. Matching names are not enough; without version identifiers, items sharing the name `license-supply-boundary` cannot simply be treated as the same object. CSHC-003 record exactly this kind of gap: the current results for adjacent entries are normal, but this entry stops before the execution record. Version distinctions were added later, but this page does not infer the cause of the break on that basis.

```text
Before migration: old entry point ─────────────> existing consumers
During trial:     old entry point ─────────────> consumers not yet migrated
                  replacement location ───────────> one confirmed consumer
After rollback:   old entry point <──────────── the consumer moved back
```

The diagram above is notation for the index; it does not mean the old entry point and the replacement location can remain in use in parallel long term. Start by routing one already identified consumer through the replacement location. The old entry point remains readable, and the rollback location is still retained. When comparing, follow the same consumer and check the results and errors from the same input, along with the state after the second call; do not mix cleaned-up screenshots with the original state. The original input, version, and first visible result should be kept with the entry.

If `forwarding` differs from the original entry point during migration, stop expanding this batch, move that consumer back to the old entry point, then check again using the original input. Here, "move back" only means restoring the entry point used before that individual migration; it does not mean the old entry point has been proven suitable for all callers. The previous version reached no conclusion on rollback scope; this version leaves that gap open as well.

The shared test environment was unavailable for a time, which blocked plans for a rerun by someone other than the original author. CSHC-001 already contain counterexamples, so results seen locally by the original author can no longer count as evidence that migration is complete. Until the environment is restored, the index can mark items that have been tried and items awaiting a rerun, but items awaiting a rerun should not be marked as migrated.

Another earlier judgment needs to be kept alongside the new audit results. CSHC-006 require labeling the earlier judgment with its context at the time, then appending the new audit results beside it; do not use the new results to overwrite the record of why the old entry point was still being retained. This makes the index look somewhat repetitive, but shows whether a conclusion was written before migration or after the replacement location had been tried.

Only when the replacement location, that consumer's confirmation, and query records for the old entry point are all still available can the item be marked complete. What is complete is one consumer's migration, not the retirement of the entire object with that name. Notes that cannot yet be traced back should remain in their old status until someone who can supply the version or execution records handles them.

The original cards for the related reruns and version checks can be found via CSHC-001, CSHC-003, and CSHC-006, respectively.
