# Dependency Boundary Entry Point Migration Process

The initial explanation retained in this index still treats `bytecode` and `effect XML` as two separate exit paths. The reason at the time was straightforward: the failure exit paths in the index file were different, and if the two sections continued to be documented as a single entry point, it would be hard to know which section to restore during a rollback. This explanation has not been deleted, because it explains why the old entry point did not disappear as soon as a replacement location appeared.

But the old explanation is also easily read as "splitting them apart completes the migration." That is not the case. During a later review, the first issue was object identity: the same-named `license-supply-boundary` had no version identifier, and identical entry point names do not prove that the same dependency is being used. The index needs to document the old object and the replacement object separately, especially when callers are still working through the old entry point. Names are only for locating entries; they cannot stand in for versions.

The main text that can currently be found is still in `docs/adj-license/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. This set of materials covers only the dependency sources, scope of adoption, and exit responsibilities associated with license. The index is not responsible for organizing all neighboring directories into a single master table; explanations that have not been traced back are left unchanged, rather than filled in as definitive conclusions using later, tidier pages.

## How the Old Entries Were Originally Arranged

The earliest version placed the old entry point on the left, treated `effect XML` as the proposed replacement location to be split out, and kept `bytecode` on the original path. `cache` was listed under unconfirmed callers. At the time, there was not enough material to determine whether it should be migrated in the same batch, nor had it been decided whether a rollback should also remove the exit path that had already been split out.

```text
Old entry point
  ├─ bytecode
  └─ effect XML    Proposed split-out location in the old records

cache: Callers not yet fully verified
```

This small diagram preserves only the arrangement at the time. It does not mean that the two exit paths have the same scope of adoption, nor that `cache` has a confirmed relationship with either exit path. Placing these names side by side in early discussions later created the impression that "the same batch had already been handled"; that impression no longer applies.

The old entry also contained the sentence "Confirm migration completion based on the actual consumers, not on whether a new entry point appears in the directory." This remains useful. A migration index is not a directory-renaming log: even if a replacement location has appeared, the old item cannot be crossed out as long as consumers remain on the old entry point, or it is still unclear which version a consumer actually corresponds to.

## The Trial Method Used Previously

During the second reorganization, the index adopted a small-batch trial approach: select one of the clearly documented consumers and switch it to the replacement location; retain the old entry point; record the results, errors, and state after the second call for the same input. The original input, version, and first visible result must be kept with that item. This approach was intended to make it possible to return to the same setup during a rollback, not to prove that all consumers were the same.

The diagram used at the time is shown below, retained here to explain how the old batches were numbered:

```text
Old entry point ─────────────> Unmigrated consumers
Replacement location ───────────> One consumer that has undergone a trial

Inconsistency occurs: Trialed item ──> Old entry point
```

"Trialed" does not mean "adoption complete." It only means that this consumer has seen a result once at the replacement location. If it is later discovered that the caller corresponds to another version with the same name, or that the documentation contains no execution record, this item must return to pending verification; the rollout must not be expanded based solely on the name on the trial path.

That version also required changing only one condition. The condition here is the entry point used by the consumer, not changing the input, version, entry point, and reorganized results all at once. If the original materials are no longer available, the index can only leave a gap; it must not reconstruct the setup at the time of migration from a reorganized page.

## Additional Notes on Execution Records

During one version check, the current results for neighboring entries were normal, while the target entry was interrupted before an execution record was created. This observation was later noted in the index, but it did not lead to a conclusion such as "the replacement location is broken." Normal neighboring entries only show that those entries were normal at the time; they cannot fill in the target item's missing version or establish which exit path the interruption occurred on.

Therefore, at least two things must be retained separately for each object with the same name in the index: the version it points to, and whether an execution record exists. With only an entry point name and not the former, it is easy to mistake the old object for the replacement object; with only a result and not the latter, it is easy to attribute a neighboring item's result to the interrupted item. These two kinds of gaps require different handling and cannot both be labeled "pending confirmation."

| Situation seen in the index | Wording retained for now |
| --- | --- |
| Objects with the same name but no version specified | List the old and replacement objects side by side; do not merge them |
| Current results exist, but execution records are missing | Note only that the results are visible, and retain the point of interruption |
| Consumers still use the old entry point | Do not mark the migration as complete |
| The replacement location is in use and the records are complete | Mark only that this consumer has undergone a trial |

This table is not a new decommissioning rule; it merely separates judgments that were mixed together in paragraphs across several earlier revisions. The old index placed "the neighboring entry is normal" and "this item can be closed out" too close together, making it read as though the latter followed from the former; they should now be evaluated against their respective records.

## Blocked Reruns

A rerun by someone other than the original author once ran into an unavailable shared test environment. The inability to reproduce results during that period was neither a successful migration nor a rejection of the replacement location; the index should only have marked the rerun as blocked at the time. Earlier, the original author's results were placed next to the entry to give the person rerunning it a reference, not to replace confirmation by another user.

This is also one reason the old entry point needs to remain readable. Once the environment is restored, the person rerunning it must be able to see the entry point used before migration, the original consumers, and the first result retained at the time. If the record of the old entry point was deleted during the trial, then even if a different result were obtained later, it would be impossible to tell whether the difference came from the replacement location, the object version, or the original input.

Here, "remain readable" is a requirement for historical operations, not a requirement for the old entry point to continue accepting new adoption. For consumers that have not migrated, the old entry point is still the current state; for consumers that have undergone a trial, the old entry point is the rollback location; for objects with the same name whose identities have not yet been fully verified, neither determination can be made on this basis.

## Returning from the Replacement Location

The old version listed a `forwarding` inconsistency as a rollback signal. This record remains: once the `forwarding` at the replacement location is inconsistent with the result retained from the original entry point, do not expand the same trial batch; first restore the consumers that have undergone the trial to the old entry point, then check again using the original input.

Here, "restore" has a precise, narrow meaning: restore the entry point used by this consumer before migration. It does not answer whether to delete the replacement location, nor whether other consumers in the same batch should also go back. Early text described rollback as though it could clear an entire batch of changes in one action; no later materials supported that scope, so that interpretation has been discarded.

After restoration, leave a record of the inconsistency observed at the time beside the original entry, rather than erasing the record of the replacement location. Otherwise, the next rerun will only show that the old entry point has been restored, not why this item did not proceed with migration. This is especially true of the attempt to split out `effect XML`: the split itself and the trial result for a particular consumer are two different records.

If the inconsistency appears only in the state after the second call, keep it in that consumer's entry as well. It must not be reduced to "the first result was normal"; the state after the second call was already part of what the trial agreed to retain. Conversely, if execution records are missing before that point, do not describe it as a `forwarding` inconsistency, because the interrupted item does not have enough records to support that judgment.

## Tracking Old Entry Points, Replacement Locations, and Consumers

The index is prone to breaking down when the three types of objects lose their boundaries after being put on the same line. This page continues to use the following tracking approach:

- **Old entry point**: Retain the name, a location that can be checked, and which consumers still enter through it. The existence of the old entry point does not mean it should still be newly adopted.
- **Replacement location**: Record which old entry it replaces. If objects with the same name have no versions, do not establish the replacement relationship definitively yet.
- **Consumer**: Record only the scope of adoption and trial status that have been observed. Do not infer consumers that have not been traced back from neighboring entries.
- **Exit criteria**: For a confirmed consumer, this migration item can be closed out only when the replacement location is available, the consumer's records are complete, and the old entry point can still be looked up.

The fourth item above comes from the operating guidance in the second version and remains suitable for reading the old batches; it is not a one-time cleanup criterion for all current objects. In particular, when versions with the same name have not been separated, the exit criteria have not even begun to be met, because "what is being replaced" has not itself been determined.

This page records the scope of adoption under each consumer, not under the entry point. An entry point can be used by multiple objects, and consumers may fall into different batches because of version differences. Assigning the scope of adoption directly to the entry point would mix the old and replacement objects together again.

## Judgments Later Retained Side by Side

The need to keep newer conclusions from overwriting older judgments is why this index remains somewhat scattered. The early judgment was: `effect XML` should be split out, while `bytecode` should remain on the old path; the intermediate judgment was: first pick one consumer for a trial, and return to the old entry point if an error occurs; the judgment added later was: entries with the same name must not be merged when version identifiers and execution records are missing.

These three sets of judgments do not address the same issue. The first deals with separating exit paths, the second with how to run trials and roll back, and the third with whether entries point to the same object. Rewriting them into a single tidy final rule would lose the constraints from the earlier and later stages, so they are still retained in the order in which they appeared.

The interpretation that "splitting it out is enough to complete migration" was later overturned; the interpretation that "a replacement location appearing is enough for decommissioning" also no longer applies. What remains usable is the practice of retaining the original input, version, first result, and state after the second call during small-batch trials, and of first restoring the trialed items when an inconsistency occurs.

What remains unresolved is not a generic "pending confirmation," but the current callers of `cache`. The old records only show that this had not been fully verified at the time; there are no materials indicating whether it belongs to `bytecode`, `effect XML`, or another object with the same name. It remains at the end of the index, without putting speculation into migration batches.

## The Closing Sequence That Still Applies

For an old entry that has already been identified, first add the version and consumers to the index, then determine the replacement location. Next, route only one consumer through the replacement location, preserving the old entry point and original setup. If the records are complete and that consumer confirms adoption, this item can be closed out; if `forwarding` is inconsistent, restore this consumer's old entry point; if the version or execution records are missing, stop at pending verification.

This sequence was retained for existing old entries; it should not be used in reverse to bring in every page with a similar name. Subsequent confirmations of individual items should change only the corresponding entries, leaving all others in their original state. DOC-38 provides only the current maintainer map; the old judgments and rollback traces for the migration batches remain on this page.

Finally, retain two gaps that were often omitted in the past:

- Current callers of `cache`: not yet fully verified.
- Whether the split-out `effect XML` should also be removed during rollback: undecided.

These gaps are more faithful to what the index could confirm at the time than a seemingly complete migration conclusion.

# Release Automation Entry Point Migration Process

This index was originally used when changing the entry point for release automation. It brought together the build queue, artifact versions, and rollback windows resulting from .github/workflows for review, but did not treat them as a single synchronized migration chain. The queue had its own schedule, artifacts had their own versions, and rollback had a separate window; the approach at the time was to have one caller that was still in use go through the alternative location first, then decide whether the old entry point could be removed.

The materials referenced by the index are still in `docs/adj-native-interop/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. This page retains the migration framing used at the time; do not treat name changes in the directory as proof that the switch has been completed. In particular, "current entry point" initially meant only the intended integration location, not that every consumer had already reached it.

```text
Old line    Current entry point-old entry point migration index ──> Old entry point
  │                 │
  │                 └── Return to the old entry point on rollback
  │
Trial line  Current entry point-old entry point migration index ──> descriptor
                                      │
                                      └── forwarding
```

The diagram above is the old representation retained on this page. It depicts `descriptor` as the new line and treats `forwarding` as a subsequent location to compare against; this is only an index relationship during migration, not an explanation of the build queue's internal implementation.

## Old Entry Point Registration

There was no unified name-mapping table for the old entry points. The earliest comparison was between continuing along `effect XML` and splitting `cache` out separately. At the time, the preference was to split out `cache`, for a very localized reason: the two sets of records in the index file had different failure exit points, and continuing to document them as the same route would obscure which side to return to during rollback.

This judgment remained on the page and could easily be read as "once cache is split out, effect XML can be decommissioned". The original record did not reach that conclusion. It only required migration batches to be tracked by actual consumer: moving one caller to the alternative location does not automatically mean another entry point with the same name can also be moved; an artifact version entering the queue does not mean the old entry point no longer has readers.

`diagnostic` was an item for which information was incomplete at the time. The old draft asked which callers were still using it, and no list was later added to this page. It therefore cannot serve as evidence that migration is complete. When a consumer is identified, record only that consumer and the entry point it uses under the same batch; do not casually draw conclusions about the remaining callers.

## Migration Sequence Used at the Time

1. Starting from the index entry point, find a caller that is still in use, and first record the artifact version it sees and the observable symptoms on failure. An alternative location appearing in the directory does not mean this step is complete.
2. Keep the old entry point and route this caller alone through `descriptor`. At this stage, observe only the return behavior, errors, and state after the second call using the original input; do not use cleaned-up page screenshots as substitute records.
3. Once `descriptor` works, connect `forwarding`. The original intent of this page was to keep the two steps separate, so that simultaneous changes to the alternative and forwarding locations would not make it impossible to tell which one skewed the results.
4. If `forwarding` does not match the old line, restore the old entry point and check again using the original input. The old draft kept this step brief: after returning to the old entry point, do not proceed to the next batch.
5. The old draft allowed maintenance of the old path to stop only if the alternative location, registered callers, and historical queries were all still usable.

Step five is the sentence on this page most prone to misuse. It came from the work plan during migration and states the threshold for being "allowed to stop maintenance", not an assertion about the system's later state. The old entry point is still treated here as a rollback target; it is not described as a historical alias that can be deleted immediately.

Migration batches are not closed out based on completion of the queue as a whole, either. A batch contains only one confirmed consumer and one action to enter the alternative location. Artifact versions may change during this period, and rollback windows may also differ; this page requires these circumstances to be kept alongside the batch, rather than collapsing multiple trials into a single green result. The original purpose was simply to ensure that, during rollback, it would still be clear which entry point to return to.

## Records Later Added in the Margins

CSHD-001 records a missing exit action. The proposed handling for that card was to add a rollback command or a stop condition to the exit action, but the decision adopted at the time was not extended to other entry points. The subsequently recorded situation was more specific: the local result had recovered, but the public entry point corresponding to the exit entry point was still failing. This observation was not used to rewrite the old sequence above; it was kept only as a side note that "local recovery" and "public entry point recovery" must not be conflated in the records.

Therefore, the statement "return to the old entry point on rollback" in the old draft does not mean that the public entry point has also recovered. At the time, it treated rollback as an entry point action, without distinguishing the local result from the public entry point's status. This wording remains because the index was once cited on that basis; that passage should not, in turn, be treated as evidence that the subsequent issues have already been resolved.

CSHD-006 instead starts with navigation from the current revision. The actual consumer needs to enter from the current revision and record the first broken-link location. The recovery page later showed green, but the exit entry point's first record was still two minutes late; the time the page turned green and the first record at the exit entry point were documented separately on two lines. This item was ultimately canceled as a legacy issue from the old environment, and no further fix was pursued in this round.

These two added notes change how the page should be read, not its original migration conclusion: a green page is not enough to replace entry point records, and being able to open the directory does not establish that the entry point has recovered during the rollback window. If the index contains only the label "recovered", still go back to the corresponding batch to see whether it refers to the local result, page status, or the first record at the exit entry point.

## Rollback Section (Original Framing Retained)

The old procedure says: if `forwarding` does not match, first restore the old entry point, then reuse the original input. Here, "restore" only means bringing the caller back to its original entry point; it does not promise that a rollback command already exists, nor does it state that the public entry point's failure will disappear as a result.

After CSHD-001 appeared, this section should have been updated to include the exit action, but it was not fully rewritten. The first step can still be taken according to the old section: stop advancing to the next batch and return to the old entry point; it cannot be used to determine that the exit entry point already has a usable rollback action. The original text is retained here to prevent later readers from mistaking "rollback" for a release capability that has already been fully validated.

Another old judgment was "confirm whether migration is complete based on actual consumers". This is more reliable than judging by the directory, but is also too coarse. It does not specify which revision the consumer entered from, does not address broken navigation links, and does not explain which to use when the page turning green and the first record do not agree. After CSHD-006, no new rules were added to this page; this gap is only flagged here.

## Items Still Handled Under the Old Index

- `effect XML`: One side of the old comparison. Do not assume it is no longer in use just because `cache` was split out.
- `cache`: The item that was favored for a separate listing at the time. That preference came from the different failure exit points, not a complete replacement decision.
- `descriptor`: The alternative location on the trial line. Callers that enter it should be kept on record by batch.
- `forwarding`: A stage compared separately after `descriptor`; if it does not match, return to the old entry point as instructed in the old draft.
- `diagnostic`: The list of callers currently using it is still incomplete, and it remains a gap in the index.

These items appearing on the same page does not mean they belong to the same change. The early records placed them in adjacent sections for ease of reference, which later created the impression that "finishing changes to any one of them is enough to end the migration". This is the main reason this page is outdated but has not yet been removed.

## Stopping Points When Using the Index

# Quality Signal Station Failed-Run Procedure

compatibility-migration-quality-signal When a failed run requiring takeover appears, start with the state left by that run rather than starting a new pass that overwrites it. The on-call entry is `docs/adj-compatibility-migration/runbooks/Compatibility-attributes-and-downlevel-storage-Quality Signal Station-Single Failed Run On-Call Page.md`; first note this run's current revision and any visible `source tree` next to the corresponding record. This is a record of one run; do not turn combinations that have not yet been run into conclusions.

## Entry

1. In the entry record, find `cache`. Note whether it is visible and whether it belongs to the same run state or only old content remains. If `cache` cannot be found, do not substitute the default location; write "cache not found" in the run record, then stop.
2. Preserve the output already produced by this run. After seeing `diagnostic`, do not clean up the run state or perform a return or recovery action yet. The most useful thing now is to record that `diagnostic` has appeared alongside the previous step's cache status, so the next shift does not see only a cleaned-up directory.
3. Check whether `identity` has appeared. If `identity` has not appeared, stop here: preserve the state of cache, diagnostic, and source tree; do not continue guessing about the descriptor, and do not invent identity information just to make the record complete.

Even if `identity` has appeared, this does not mean the run succeeded. After noting where it appeared, mark only `descriptor` as the checkpoint requiring further verification in this run. If someone continues later, they may only pick up from the same run-state record; without new observations, do not rewrite this run's failure assessment.

## Single Rerun

When a rerun is needed, change only one condition per trial. The run record must clearly state the condition changed in this attempt, whether the cache was reused, whether the diagnostic appeared again, and the identity result. Do not replace multiple conditions at once and then work backward from the final output to infer the cause; combinations not tested remain unknown. If the new run does not preserve the previous run's state, record it separately as a new failure sample; do not overwrite the original record.

The current revision is an identifier that must accompany every rerun. The next shift needs it to distinguish old cache from content produced by this run; without a revision, do not combine the results of the two runs. Retain the descriptor only as a verification checkpoint; do not interpret it on this page as meaning that recovery has been completed.

## Stop and Handoff

Stop in any of these cases: the cache cannot be found, the run state has been cleaned up after the diagnostic appeared, identity is missing, or the rerun changed more than one condition at once. Stopping is not a cleanup action after a failure; preserve visible output and record the step at which the stop occurred.

The handoff record must include at least the current revision, source tree, whether the cache was found, whether the diagnostic appeared, the identity status, and whether the descriptor has been marked. The recovery action has not yet been tried in the shared environment, so the old entry point and return action in the rollback section remain in place for verification under different permission levels only; they do not constitute a validated recovery result.

# Release Branch Cut Deviation Postmortem

During the release branch cut window, the visible result did not appear as originally scheduled. What was seen first was a mismatch between the schedule and the result; at the time, it was not possible to distinguish whether the deviation lay in the branch cut, runner queueing, or subsequent retries.

## Shift Timeline

- During the window, the first discovery was that the visible result had diverged from the original schedule. The initial checks focused on this discrepancy; it was not directly recorded as a branch-content issue.
- A targeted fixture run was then retained. It was used only to recheck the result in that window and did not cover all release paths.
- After the temporary recovery, the visible result in the window realigned with the original schedule. The recovery status was therefore recorded as complete during the shift, but no root cause was written on that basis.
- At handoff, one sentence was added: the runner queue has a published retry note. This was the control point added this time, to avoid treating a retry state in the queue as an undocumented wait.

## Impact and Assessment at the Time

Impact was recorded only as the visible result being out of alignment within this window. It was not confirmed whether the deviation changed the release branch's content or whether it changed only when the result appeared; both explanations remained open at the time.

The temporary recovery was once understood as "the window schedule had been restored." This wording is retained here because it reflects the scope of what was observed during the shift: what was seen after recovery was the result reappearing, not a complete explanation of runner behavior or the branch-cut process. When citing this page later, this old assessment should not be read as saying that the root cause had already been identified.

This record separates three points in time: first, the visible result deviated; then, a targeted fixture run was performed; finally, the temporary recovery occurred. The recovery happened after the recheck action and does not allow us to infer that the recheck explained the deviation; the retry note in the queue only supplemented the record visible at the time and is insufficient on its own to show which step caused the delay.

## Open Items

Evidence is still missing to connect the initial deviation, the queue retry record, and the temporary recovery into a single causal chain. The targeted fixture run can only show that the recheck was performed; it cannot show that failure to reproduce means the original schedule was always correct. Whether the branch content actually changed and whether the deviation affected only when the result appeared remain undetermined in this window's record.

# Descriptor Migration Window FAQ

This page was originally used to answer ad hoc questions during the migration window. The old version is still retained above: it treated the compatibility-migration entry point as evidence that the candidate path had been verified, and treated "having a rerunnable command" as sufficient to close a discussion. Both claims later caused misunderstandings.

**What exactly does the existing compatibility-migration entry point prove?**

It only proves that this migration issue has a retained entry point, or that someone once brought a candidate path here for discussion. It doesn't prove that the path was actually reviewed, nor that descriptor migration has been completed. If all that's under the entry point is secondhand reports, old links, or a comment saying "already looked at it," the candidate path should still be treated as unconfirmed; don't use that as grounds to close the other questions in the window as well.

**Who is responsible when a candidate path is withdrawn?**

No fixed person is designated here to handle withdrawals. The withdrawal record must name the person actually responsible for the review; the proposer may explain why they aren't continuing the attempt, but that doesn't automatically entitle them to close the discussion. The previous version's "the reviewer can close it after seeing the record" no longer applies, because it did not require the person responsible for the review and the boundary evidence to be recorded together.

The rule the team used afterward for closing threads was: Close a thread only after a reproducible command, its positive or negative boundary, and the responsible reviewer are recorded together.

This requires all three to be present together. Someone else must be able to rerun the command; the positive or negative boundary must show whether this run supports the candidate path or rules it out; the person responsible for the review can't be identified only in conversation. If any of the three is missing, logging can continue during the window, but that item cannot be treated as closed.

**How can we respond when there is no targeted fixture run?**

You can record "no targeted fixture run obtained yet" and keep the question itself. Don't use the existence of an entry point, a successful general run, or a withdrawal to supply an affirmative answer. This gap has not been resolved on this page; the old version treated it as a detail that didn't need to be listed separately, which later proved inappropriate.

If you see the short answers in the first two versions, read them as the guidance used at the time. They explain why some people thought the entry point was sufficient then; they no longer provide grounds for closure.
